articles.title: Inquérito das fake news: Fachin determina arquivamento | G1
articles.standfirst: Inquérito foi aberto em março de 2019 para apurar ataques e ameaças aos ministros e ao STF. Desdobramentos da investigação que estiverem abertos seguirão em análise de forma individual.
articles.summary: Inquérito foi aberto em março de 2019 para apurar ataques e ameaças aos ministros e ao STF. Desdobramentos da investigação que estiverem abertos seguirão em análise de forma individual.
articles.body:
O presidente do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ), Edson Fachin , determinou nesta segunda-feira (9) o arquivamento do inquérito das fake news , aberto há mais de sete anos e que apurou ataques e ameaças a integrantes da Corte.

Apesar do encerramento do chamado "inquérito-mãe", desdobramentos dessa investigação que estiverem abertos seguirão em análise de forma individual no STF.

"O que ora se encerra é o procedimento investigatório matriz, deixando-se, a partir desta decisão, de se realizar a distribuição por prevenção da investigação de fatos novos supervenientes relacionados a seu objeto originário. Não se apaga sua história, não se infirmam as razões institucionais que determinaram sua instauração, nem se desconhece a relevância que teve para a proteção desta Corte e da ordem constitucional em momento singular da vida republicana", diz Fachin na decisão.

Na decisão, o presidente do STF determina que dados sensíveis do material reunido ao longo de mais de 12 mil páginas e 50 volumes sejam separados, e diz que após isso, levantará o sigilo do inquérito.

"Acolhendo a manifestação da PGR, o sigilo dos autos será mantido provisoriamente até a conclusão do procedimento de desentranhamento e separação de documentos que contenham dados sensíveis e protegidos pelo direito à intimidade, como sigilos bancário, fiscal, telefônico e dados pessoais. Concluída a triagem e criado um apenso específico, o sigilo do inquérito será levantado", diz nota do STF.

Fachin atendeu a um pedido da Procuradoria-Geral da República (PGR) , que entendeu ter esgotado o objeto específico.

O ministro afirma ainda que a decisão não alcança condenações, absolvições, acordos, decisões de recebimento de denúncia ou demais pronunciamentos jurisdicionais "proferidos em processos autônomos, cuja validade e eficácia não constituem objeto deste pronunciamento".

Ao justificar o arquivamento, Fachin afirmou que uma investigação que, "depois de mais de sete anos, permanece aberta à agregação de fatos e procedimentos supervenientes distancia-se de sua natureza preparatória".

"Inexiste fundamento para que uma investigação permaneça indefinidamente aberta a acontecimentos futuros: a complexidade justifica o tempo indispensável à elucidação de fatos determinados, não legitimando a ausência de termo final nem a renovação permanente de seu objeto".

"Reconhece-se, simplesmente, que investigações, precisamente porque instrumentais, devem encontrar termo. A proteção das instituições democráticas, não menos que a persecução daqueles que atentem contra elas, há de realizar-se dentro da Constituição. É essa mesma Constituição que protege a independência do Poder Judiciário e que assegura a todos a razoável duração do processo, a liberdade e o devido processo legal", afirma Fachin.

🔎 O inquérito das fake news foi aberto em março de 2019 por iniciativa do então presidente do Supremo, Dias Toffoli, que designou Alexandre de Moraes como relator.

O foco inicial era apurar ataques e ameaças aos ministros e ao STF, mas ao longo dos anos o inquérito teve seu objeto ampliado e alcançou até mesmo um integrante da Corte: o ministro André Mendonça.

A apuração reúne operações policiais, bloqueios de redes sociais, prisões e acusações oferecidas pela Procuradoria-Geral da República. Além disso, virou alvo de críticas de entidades, como a Ordem dos Advogados do Brasil, e motivo de atritos principalmente com a oposição no Congresso, além de provocar desconforto no meio jurídico.

O fim do inquérito das fake news começou a ser discutido internamente ainda na presidência do ministro aposentado Luis Roberto Barroso. Em conversas reservadas, Barroso vinha debatendo com o ministro Alexandre de Moraes, a conclusão do inquérito. Moraes mostrava resistência.

Com a saída de Barroso, Fachin assumiu as tratativas internas para o fim do inquérito, já no fim do ano passado. O presidente do Supremo defendia que era preciso encontrar um prazo razoável.

Fachin foi relator da ação que, em junho de 2020, levou o Supremo a declarar a legalidade e constitucionalidade do inquérito, aberto para investigar a existência de notícias fraudulentas (fake news), denunciações caluniosas e ameaças contra a Corte, seus ministros e familiares.

A crise institucional instalada no STF pelos desdobramentos do caso Master, no entanto, acabou pressionando Moraes e levando Fachin a assumir, em setembro, a condução do desfecho do inquérito. Fachin determinou um pente-fino em todo o inquérito.

104 procedimentos vinculados ao inquérito;

Diligências sem cumprimento há 22 meses, como a tomada de depoimentos;

12 mil páginas, mais de 50 volumes, que reúnem dados pessoais, bancários, fiscais e empresariais de pessoas físicas, instituições e pessoas jurídicas.

Presidente do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), ministro Edson Fachin. — Foto: Antonio Augusto/STF

No pedido de arquivamento feito ao Supremo , a PGR defendeu o inquérito.

"Ameaças dirigidas aos ministros e a seus familiares, campanhas de desinformação financiadas e difundidas em massa e incitações ao fechamento do Tribunal voltavam-se contra a liberdade de decidir e a autoridade das decisões; projetavam, enfim, as suas repercussões sobre a preservação da ordem constitucional", afirmou a PGR.

O procurador-geral, Paulo Gonet, também apontou que a extensão do inquérito foi uma necessidade diante dos riscos.

"A extensão temporal deste inquérito encontrou correspondência na sucessão de ameaças que, ao longo de sete anos, foram identificadas às condições de livre e independente exercício da função jurisdicional pelos integrantes do Supremo Tribunal Federal", declarou.

Na avaliação da Procuradoria, o levantamento integral do sigilo do inquérito tem potencial para causar uma exposição negativa, sendo que a Constituição admite a restrição da publicidade para defender a intimidade ou o interesse social.

"O interesse público em conhecer fatos relevantes para a vida comunitária se encontra, aqui, atendido pela publicidade das ações penais e das decisões respectivas. Não há presumir, entretanto, que semelhante interesse prepondere sobre a proteção devida aos dados e à privacidade de quem atravessou a investigação sem a cristalização de indícios suspeitos. Aqui, é forçosa a apreciação casuística dos dados a serem abertos", disse.

articles.title: PGR e Judiciário pedem R$ 533 milhões para pagar penduricalhos | G1
articles.standfirst: Justiça Federal disse precisar de R$ 208,9 milhões e Ministério Público da União de R$ 324 milhões em 2026; AGU pediu que STF diga como despesas serão pagas diante da falta de recursos.
articles.summary: A AGU acionou o STF após a PGR e o Judiciário pedirem R$ 533 milhões extras para pagar penduricalhos e bônus de antiguidade diante da falta de verba no Orçamento.
articles.body:
A Procuradoria-Geral da República (PGR) e o Conselho da Justiça Federal (CJF) informaram ao governo federal que precisam de cerca de R$ 533 milhões adicionais em 2026 para bancar o pagamento de benefícios decorrentes de decisões do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ).

Segundo os documentos enviados à Advocacia-Geral da União (AGU), a Justiça Federal calcula uma necessidade adicional de R$ 208,9 milhões, enquanto o Ministério Público da União (MPU) estima um impacto de R$ 324 milhões. Os valores somados chegam a R$ 532,9 milhões.

Após receber as demandas, a AGU levou a questão ao STF e pediu que a Corte esclareça como as decisões deverão ser cumpridas diante da alegada falta de recursos no Orçamento.

O órgão não pede diretamente ao Supremo a liberação dos R$ 533 milhões. Solicita que os ministros indiquem como o julgamento deve ser cumprido e determinem as providências orçamentárias necessárias para viabilizar os pagamentos.

O impasse envolve principalmente a Parcela de Valorização por Tempo de Antiguidade na Carreira (PVTAC), benefício reconhecido pelo STF para integrantes da magistratura e do Ministério Público, autorizada pelo STF em março no julgamento dos penduricalhos.

💰 A parcela corresponde a 5% do subsídio a cada cinco anos de efetivo exercício em atividade jurídica, limitada a 35%.

O STF estabeleceu que a PVTAC poderia compor a remuneração de magistrados e membros do Ministério Público enquanto não fosse editada a lei nacional prevista na Constituição para disciplinar as verbas indenizatórias.

Posteriormente, ao analisar recursos apresentados pela PGR, o STF determinou a implantação imediata da parcela, inclusive para inativos e pensionistas, sem a necessidade de requerimento dos interessados.

O Supremo também autorizou a possibilidade de pagamento de outras parcelas, entre elas indenizações por férias e licenças-prêmio não usufruídas por interesse público e auxílio-saúde mediante reembolso, observados os limites estabelecidos na decisão.

No documento, o órgão afirma que Judiciário e Ministério Público estão, de um lado, diante de uma determinação de implantação imediata da PVTAC e da autorização para pagamento das demais parcelas e, de outro, alegam não ter dotação orçamentária suficiente para suportar as despesas.

Por isso, a AGU diz considerar "imprescindível" uma orientação do STF sobre a forma correta de cumprir a decisão.

Ao final, pede que a Corte esclareça como o julgamento deverá ser executado diante da insuficiência orçamentária e determine as providências necessárias para o cumprimento das obrigações impostas pelas decisões do próprio STF.

O CJF comunicou à AGU que os efeitos financeiros das decisões não foram contemplados na elaboração do Orçamento porque os julgamentos ocorreram posteriormente.

O órgão argumenta que a suplementação é necessária para cumprir as decisões sem retirar recursos de outras despesas consideradas essenciais ao funcionamento da Justiça Federal.

O CJF defende a edição de uma medida provisória para abertura de crédito extraordinário ainda em 2026.

Também pede que sejam previstos recursos no Orçamento de 2027 porque considera essas despesas de caráter permanente.

Ministério do Planejamento viu obstáculo

Antes de a questão chegar ao Supremo, a consultoria jurídica do Ministério do Planejamento analisou a possibilidade de abertura de crédito extraordinário para bancar os gastos do MPU.

O parecer reconheceu que o cumprimento da decisão judicial é obrigatório, mas concluiu que a origem judicial da despesa, sozinha, não é suficiente para justificar a abertura de crédito extraordinário.

🔎 Pela Constituição Federal, esse instrumento é reservado a despesas imprevisíveis e urgentes. Entre os exemplos previstos no texto constitucional estão guerra, comoção interna e calamidade pública.

A área jurídica do Planejamento afirmou que, diferentemente de outros casos analisados pelo STF, a decisão sobre os benefícios da magistratura e do Ministério Público não determinou expressamente a abertura de crédito extraordinário.

Segundo o parecer, seria necessária uma decisão judicial específica que analisasse o instrumento orçamentário e autorizasse ou determinasse a adoção das medidas necessárias para a abertura desse tipo de crédito.

Foi a partir desse entendimento que PGR e CJF procuraram a AGU. O procurador-geral da República, Paulo Gonet, pediu ao advogado-geral da União, Jorge Messias, que adotasse as providências necessárias para levar a questão ao Judiciário.

Gonet citou a conclusão da consultoria jurídica do Ministério do Planejamento de que seria necessária uma decisão judicial tratando especificamente da abertura de crédito extraordinário. O presidente do CJF, ministro Luis Felipe Salomão, encaminhou pedido semelhante à AGU.

Salomão afirmou que a falta de recursos pode provocar atrasos ou insuficiência nos pagamentos, novos questionamentos judiciais e pressão sobre outras despesas da Justiça Federal.

Fachada do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), em Brasília, com estátua da Justiça em destaque. — Foto: Divulgação/STF

articles.title: Fachin mantém sigilo de dados sensíveis do inquérito das fake news; PGR queria reserva integral | G1
articles.standfirst: Aberto há sete anos, inquérito foi arquivado pelo presidente do STF nesta segunda-feira (9).
articles.summary: Aberto há sete anos, inquérito foi arquivado pelo presidente do STF nesta segunda-feira (9).
articles.body:
Presidente do Supremo Tribunal Fedreal (STF), ministro Edson Fachin — Foto: Antonio Augusto/STF

O presidente do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), Edson Fachin, decidiu nesta segunda-feira (9) manter o sigilo parcial dos dados reunidos ao longo de sete anos de investigação do inquérito das fake news.

⚖️ Aberto há mais de sete anos para apurar ataques e ameaças a integrantes do STF, o inquérito das fakes news foi arquivado por Fachin.

Os arquivos da investigação somam mais de 12 mil páginas, 57 volumes e mais de 100 anexos.

De acordo com a decisão de Fachin, serão preservadas informações sensíveis, que envolvam a intimidade e a vida privada de investigados e de autoridades públicas mencionadas na investigação.

Depois de separadas, o STF deverá deve levantar o sigilo das informações no âmbito do inquérito.

"Em atenção à manifestação da Procuradoria-Geral da República a respeito do sigilo dos autos e a necessidade de serem resguardados dados relacionados à intimidade e vida privada de pessoas e autoridades públicas mencionadas ao longo das apurações, cuja proteção encontra fundamento de legitimidade no art. 5º, X e LXXIX, da Constituição Federal, no art. 31, § 1º, I, da Lei n. 12.527/2011, e nos arts. 2º, IV e 6º, III e VII, da Lei n. 13.709/2018, o sigilo dos autos deverá ser mantido até a formação de apenso com publicidade restrita para resguardar tais direitos", escreveu Fachin na decisão.

Segundo o ministro, após a conclusão desse procedimento, "levante-se, imediatamente o sigilo dos autos [processo]", como previsto na Constituição Federal.

A posição de Fachin contraria a do procurador-geral da República, Paulo Gonet, para quem a investigação envolveu um grande número de pessoas cujas informações deveriam ser preservadas.

"O acervo reunido nestes autos ao longo de 7 anos guarda informações de elevada sensibilidade estratégica, relativas à segurança estrutural e institucional dos Ministros do Tribunal e de altas autoridades da República. Os autos registram ameaças e elementos atinentes à integridade física e operacional de agentes públicos no exercício de funções centrais do Estado; a sua divulgação tem o potencial de expor ao espaço público cogitadas vulnerabilidades que a investigação buscou proteger", escreveu Gonet.

De acordo com a PGR, em mais de 50 volumes, há dados pessoais, bancários e fiscais de empresas, instituições e investigados.

"Este inquérito ultrapassa a marca das 12 mil folhas e reúne um amplo universo de pessoas, potencializando os riscos concretos de afetação da própria segurança das autoridades protegidas e o direito fundamental de pessoas com relação a quem é dado presumir não terem interesse em ver os seus dados atirados a ampla exibição pública", acrescentou o PGR.

Na avaliação da PGR, a divulgação de todas as informações do inquérito poderia expor negativamente pessoas citadas na investigação. A PGR argumentou que a Constituição permite restringir o acesso a essas informações para proteger a intimidade das pessoas ou o interesse social.

Gonet afirmou ainda que as pessoas e empresas mencionadas poderiam pedir diretamente acesso aos elementos do inquérito.

articles.title: Opinion - Losing Congress won’t make Trump a lame duck — it will make him a wrecking ball
articles.summary: Trump has shown us what he’s willing to do and how he bends the rules when his party controls Congress. But we ain’t seen nothing yet.
articles.body:
Last week, America delivered a resounding defeat to President Trump's MAGA agenda . Trump has since vacillated in response to the results, saying that "the Democrats did a good job " and that he will work with them, while also threatening to use his " tremendous powers " to veto Democratic policies.

Trump has shown us what he's willing to do and how he bends the rules when his party controls Congress. But we ain't seen nothing yet.

Historical precedent and conventional political wisdom say that Trump losing control of Congress will relegate him to the ultimate ignominy of being a lame-duck president presiding over a divided government. That's unlikely to be Trump's fate.

Counterintuitively, losing the midterms may keep Trump popularly relevant and save him from the usual presidential fade into oblivion. While he'll get less and less cooperation from Capitol Hill, he'll be relatively released from the burdens of governing and free to pursue the attention that he so desperately craves. For Trump, the surest way to get that attention is to pick a fight.

Losing the midterms won't make Trump weaker — it will only make him more aggressive.

Part of the reason is temperament: Governing is hard , and Trump has always been more at home at the rally podium than behind the Resolute Desk. That preference has been indulged more often this term: loyalists have replaced the first administration's "adults in the room," and Trump doesn't have another election ahead of him — at least, not a constitutional one — to moderate him.

Government institutions and groups within those institutions like the YOLO Caucus , made up of senators freed from reelection considerations, have somewhat constrained Trump thus far. Earlier this year, for instance, Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) blocked the confirmation of a new Fed chair until Trump dropped his punitive investigation of Jerome Powell .

There is always the possibility that Trump will roll over and go along with traditionally Democratic policies. But with no hope of exerting substantive control over a Democratic Congress for the remainder of his time in office, it is more likely that Trump will soon become essentially unfettered — a YOLO president, if you will.

Thus far, a friendly legislative branch has constrained him only at the margins. Even with his party in control, Trump prefers the bull-in-a-china-shop approach. And when that approach is stymied, he has waded into defying Congress outright, offering only token, narrow deference when the legal ambiguity can't be pushed any further.

In February, Trump launched the Iran war without congressional authorization . When the 60-day War Powers Resolution deadline arrived, his administration argued that an April ceasefire had ended the clock . When the ceasefire collapsed in July, he sent a notice calling the renewed strikes a separate operation, restarting the clock .

For two straight years , the White House has canceled money that Congress appropriated by letting the funds expire before lawmakers could vote on the request. The Government Accountability Office has twice found this type of "pocket rescission" illegal .

We also have seen what happens when the legislature isn't so friendly. Trump lost the House once before , and the two years that followed gave us the then-longest-ever government shutdown , a national emergency declaration to spend border wall money Congress refused to authorize, and two impeachments .

This Democratic Congress will end any chance of his legislative priorities passing. Holding the purse strings on every spending bill, it will also provide a useful foil to Trump and will likely supercharge his use of executive orders — or straight-up defiance of Congress. Most usefully for Trump, it will give him a seemingly reasonable justification with presidential precedent: The legislature is gridlocked, so he has to act alone, using the same " pen and phone " argument Barack Obama made when lawmakers stalled him.

The next two years of Democrats' subpoenas and appropriations oversight will likely be embarrassing and painful, but as the border wall " emergency " showed, they'll have limited actual effect. Impeachment will likely be on the docket at some point. But without the requisite 67 votes to convict and remove Trump from office, a third impeachment will be no more damaging than the first two — and it will give him a major grievance to trumpet at every rally.

With policy accomplishments off the table, grievance will be the only option for Trump to stay popularly relevant, exert control over his faithful, and bask in the adoration of his base as a martyr for the cause. Without a willing legislative partner acquiescing to his efforts to redefine America and the president's role in it, Trump will be backed into a corner where the only option he sees is to fight harder than ever.

If and when that happens, Trump will be where he's most effective and, seemingly, most comfortable. He can leave behind the need to pretend to care about governing and simply go on another tour, raging against everything Democrats do and breaking whatever vestiges are left of our national institutions and decency.

We've already seen what Trump does with a Congress that goes along with him. Now we're about to find out what he does with a Congress that won't.

Micah Ables writes about foreign policy and U.S. politics at Conscience of a Young Conservative .

articles.title: Trump after meeting with Qatari PM says he believes war with Iran is militarily 'effectively over'
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Monday told reporters he believes the war in Iran “militarily is effectively over," suggesting that — at least fo...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Monday told reporters he believes the war in Iran "militarily is effectively over," suggesting that — at least for now — he's not prepared to resume the bombardment that has devastated the Islamic Republic and caused reverberations across the global economy.

The president made a surprise visit to the White House briefing room after meeting earlier in the day with Qatar's prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani.

"Iran militarily is effectively over," Trump said. "We're just keeping it the status quo."

He added that Iran has been "decapitated" but said he is still looking to make sure there's a long-term solution to ensuring that Iran's nuclear program is defanged.

It was some of Trump's most definitive comments about moving away from his threat to resume strikes on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections had passed.

The president's Republican Party lost both chambers of Congress to Democrats in last week's elections. The elections were shadowed by dissatisfaction among the American electorate over the 8-month-old war, which has led to a surge in fuel prices that's impacted nearly ever sector of the global economy.

Trump, over the course of the conflict, has repeatedly said he is on the cusp of ordering U.S. forces to escalate attacks if Iran's leaders don't quickly agree to U.S. terms to end the war, only to back down. In earlier cycles, he has also edged away with a last-minute declaration, sometimes at the behest of Gulf allies, that he's going to give diplomacy more time.

In a posting on social media shortly before speaking to reporters, Trump once again asserted that Middle East allies — Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait and others — "would prefer the status quo." Minutes later, in his exchange with reporters, he sought to assure war-weary Americans that there was "positive momentum" and that he saw a "good chance" that the war "could get ended."

"They're talking to us, and they're talking very politely, And we'll see what happens," Trump said. He added, "The military action doesn't seem to be a very necessary thing, but we're locked and loaded, ready to go for any reason that changes."

Trump, however, gave no hint of a drawdown of the thousands of U.S. troops who have been shifted to the waters off of Iran and maintain a naval blockade to stem the flow of Iranian oil into the global market.

"We're keeping it going. We have the greatest military blockade ever," Trump said.

Qatari officials last week presented proposals on Iran's nuclear program, according to two Middle East government officials familiar with the matter who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

The White House declined to comment, though Trump last week alluded to ongoing indirect talks with Tehran.

All the while, Tehran continues to insist on several concessions from the U.S., which Trump has declined in the past. Among the core demands Iran says must be met before engaging in nuclear talks: ending the U.S. blockade on Iran's ports , lifting sanctions, unfreezing its assets, issuing compensation for war damage and ending hostilities throughout the region, including Israeli operations in Lebanon.

Earlier Monday, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has come under fire over the conflict, said the next steps on the war are up to Trump, including the possibility of telling Iran: "Hey, we're done, and we're going to watch your nuclear material. You better not move it."

The defense secretary has been one of the administration's most prominent defenders of the war. Critics say the administration launched the war without proper authorization, violated the War Powers Resolution and subverted congressional war-declaring powers.

Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky moved Monday to force a vote to impeach Hegseth , largely over his execution of the war.

Trump told CNN in a phone interview Sunday that as long as the U.S. sees progress in negotiations with the Iranians and they sign a "strong agreement," it's "highly unlikely it's going to be necessary" to resume strikes.

Trump said, however, that the U.S. had identified infrastructure targets, including 38 bridges, that it would strike if military action resumes.

The U.S. military, meanwhile, still has carried out limited strikes on Iran , including against its air defenses, at least twice over the past week. It also fired on and disabled a commercial ship Saturday that the U.S. says was trying to breach its naval blockade on Iranian ports.

AP writers Konstantin Toropin, Samy Magdy and Seung Min Kim contributed reporting.

articles.title: STJ criou sistemas para reforçar segurança após suspeita de vazamento por ex-servidor | G1
articles.standfirst: Humberto Pradera, ex-secretário de TI do STJ, foi alvo de mandado de prisão em operação que investiga suspeita de acesso indevido do advogado Willer Tomaz, amigo de Flávio Bolsonaro, a informações de processos na Corte.
articles.summary: Humberto Pradera, ex-secretário de TI do STJ, foi alvo de mandado de prisão em operação que investiga suspeita de acesso indevido do advogado Willer Tomaz, amigo de Flávio Bolsonaro, a informações de processos na Corte.
articles.body:
O Superior Tribunal de Justiça (STJ) criou dois novos sistemas de segurança após a descoberta de uma suspeita de vazamento de informações da Corte para o advogado Willer Tomaz, amigo de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL).

Humberto Fontoura Pradera, ex-secretário de Tecnologia da Informação do STJ, foi alvo de mandado de prisão nesta terça-feira (10) sob suspeita de ter facilitado o acesso indevido de Willer Tomaz a informações de processos que tramitam na Corte.

Antes da ordem de prisão desta terça, Pradera já havia sido alvo de busca e apreensão em 19 de outubro, na primeira fase da Operação Linceu.

A investigação encontrou no celular de Willer uma foto enviada por Pradera de um documento que ainda estava em produção no STJ.

Diante do episódio, o tribunal reforçou seus protocolos de segurança, com mudanças em senhas e acessos, adoção de dupla autenticação e novas restrições para evitar vazamentos de informações.

➡️ Internamente, o STJ considerou o caso grave e determinou a adoção de novos controles nos sistemas .

As ferramentas buscam não apenas aumentar a segurança, mas também ampliar a capacidade de identificar quem acessou determinada informação e rastrear eventuais vazamentos. O modelo é chamado internamente de “confiança auditável”.

O STJ também determinou como padrão a elaboração de um inventário dos acessos, com registros que permitam o rastreamento das informações.

Os mecanismos incluem ainda a identificação de textos ocultos e metadados, autenticação mais resistente e monitoramento do uso dos dados.

articles.title: Taciba decreta emergência após vendaval destruir recinto | G1
articles.standfirst: Decreto publicado nesta segunda-feira (9) tem validade de 60 dias e autoriza contratações emergenciais para recuperar áreas atingidas. Reconstrução do recinto pode custar mais de R$ 7 milhões.
articles.summary: Taciba decreta emergência após vendaval de 100 km/h destruir o recinto de exposições e destelhar casas; reconstrução da estrutura custará R$ 7 milhões.
articles.body:
A Prefeitura de Taciba (SP) decretou situação de emergência nas áreas atingidas pelo temporal do último sábado (7), quando rajadas de vento de até 100 km/h derrubaram a cobertura do Recinto de Exposições José Cardoso de Pádua, destelharam casas e provocaram outros estragos no município.

A medida foi oficializada nesta segunda-feira (9), por meio do decreto nº 392, assinado pelo prefeito Izidoro Ricci ( PP ) e publicado no Diário Oficial.

De acordo com o documento, as chuvas intensas e as fortes rajadas de vento causaram danos em vias públicas, prédios municipais, residências, edificações, estradas rurais e acessos, além de quedas de árvores e problemas na rede elétrica.

Estrutura do recinto de exposições de Taciba (SP) desabou por causa da força dos ventos, com rajadas de até 100 km/h, no sábado (7): Defesa Civil faz rescaldo nesta segunda (9) — Foto: Aline Costa/TV TEM

Além dos danos no recinto, oito casas na zona rural foram destelhadas. Na área urbana, o muro um muro do Estádio Municipal Azarias Ozório dos Reis desabou. Também houve queda de árvores e pontos de alagamento. A TV TEM esteve no município nesta segunda (9) conferindo os estragos.

O decreto classifica o fenômeno como desastre súbito do tipo “ tempestade local/convectiva – vendaval ”, conforme a Classificação e Codificação Brasileira de Desastres (Cobrade).

Muro do estádio municipal de Taciba (SP) desabou por causa de temporal de sábado (7), com ventos de 100 km/h, segundo a Defesa Civil municipal — Foto: Aline Costa/TV TEM

A situação de emergência tem validade de 60 dias, com efeitos retroativos a 7 de novembro, data em que o temporal atingiu a cidade.

A medida autoriza a mobilização de todos os órgãos municipais necessários para atuar nas ações de resposta ao desastre, na recuperação das áreas afetadas e na reconstrução dos locais danificados, sob coordenação da Defesa Civil municipal.

Funcionários da Prefeitura de Taciba (SP) realizam nesta segunda (9) — Foto: Aline Costa/TV TEM

Com a declaração de emergência, a Prefeitura também fica autorizada a realizar contratações diretas, com dispensa de licitação, para a compra de materiais, prestação de serviços e execução de obras estritamente necessárias ao atendimento da situação emergencial.

O decreto determina que sejam respeitados os requisitos e limites previstos na legislação.

O documento ainda autoriza a abertura de crédito extraordinário para cobrir despesas urgentes e imprescindíveis relacionadas à resposta ao desastre.

Outra medida prevista é a convocação de voluntários e a realização de campanhas para arrecadar recursos destinados à assistência da população atingida. As ações deverão ser coordenadas pela Coordenadoria Municipal de Proteção e Defesa Civil.

O decreto também prevê que, em caso de risco iminente, autoridades responsáveis pelas ações de resposta poderão entrar em imóveis para prestar socorro ou determinar a evacuação imediata.

O uso de propriedades particulares também poderá ser autorizado diante de perigo público, com previsão de indenização posterior ao proprietário caso haja danos.

Em Taciba (SP) a força da chuva causou a queda de um muro e destelhou a cobertura do Recinto de Exposições José Cardoso de Pádua. — Foto: Defesa Civil/Divulgação

Recinto de exposições teve cobertura destruída

O vendaval que atingiu Taciba no sábado provocou o desabamento de grande parte da estrutura do Recinto de Exposições José Cardoso de Pádua.

O espaço, utilizado para eventos, festas e atividades com crianças e adolescentes, havia recebido os rodeios e shows sertanejos da Expo Taciba uma semana antes do temporal.

Segundo a Defesa Civil municipal, as rajadas de vento chegaram a 100 km/h. O coordenador do órgão, Edivaldo Souza, comparou a intensidade do fenômeno à passagem de um pequeno ciclone. A chuva durou cerca de uma hora.

A construção da estrutura do recinto custou aproximadamente R$ 3 milhões, há três anos. Para reconstruí-la atualmente, a estimativa apresentada pela Prefeitura é de mais de R$ 7 milhões. Ainda não há previsão para a recuperação do espaço.

articles.title: Fim do inquérito das fake news fecha um foco de crise no STF, mas caso Master ainda mantém tribunal sob tensão | G1
articles.body:
O fim do inquérito das fake news demorou . Veio mais de sete anos depois de sua abertura, mas fecha um foco de crise dentro do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF).

Responsável pela decisão, o presidente do STF, Edson Fachin, tem pela frente outro ponto de tensão: o caso Master.

Mas ainda tem outro desafio para debelar as crises que enfrenta em sua presidência: levar ao plenário a discussão sobre se ministros do tribunal serão investigados pelo envolvimento com o ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro.

Sobre os três recaem as maiores suspeitas de uma relação além do recomendável entre magistrados do Supremo e um ex-banqueiro hoje preso.

Além de Moraes, Nunes Marques e Toffoli, também foram citados André Mendonça, Luiz Fux e Gilmar Mendes. Esses, porém, sem conteúdo comprometedor.

Caberá ao plenário do STF analisar o relatório e decidir o que fazer em cada caso. Há uma cobrança para que os casos mais complicados e suspeitos sejam submetidos a uma investigação da própria PF. Uma ala do Supremo trabalha para arquivar tudo e, com isso, tentar debelar a crise interna.

No caso do inquérito das fake news, Fachin arquivou o inquérito-mãe, o 4.781, mas ainda será preciso analisar se 95 procedimentos derivados dele também serão arquivados.

O encerramento do inquérito-mãe acaba com o poder que ele conferia a Alexandre de Moraes de abrir novos procedimentos derivados da investigação principal. O que já virou ação penal segue com Moraes até o julgamento.

Presidente do Supremo arquiva definitivamente o inquérito das fake news — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

articles.title: Faisal Islam: What the boss of US tech giant Nvidia told me about China and national security
articles.summary: Huang, who is now being investigated over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, is far more important to the future of the world order than other tech bosses.
articles.body:
Jensen Huang has the air of the late Steve Jobs about him. I have interviewed both, and the up-close charisma - and occasionally scratchy genius - is shared.

Both sported a signature item of black clothing, although Huang opts for a leather jacket rather than the Apple founder's turtle neck.

Both are innovators revered in the tech world. However, Huang is now being investigated over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy .

Everything you have heard about Artificial Intelligence (AI) over the past few months - good, bad, revolutionary and catastrophic - is dependent on having the most powerful frontier AI models.

In turn they depend on the most powerful microchips, and for years that has been this very company, Nvidia, led by Huang, and his technology rooted in repurposed games graphics and the manufacturing prowess of Taiwan.

Names such as Gracehopper, Vera and Rubin mean almost nothing to the public, but are the names of chips powering the creation of AI models transforming the world.

I met Huang as he held court with reporters and offered words of encouragement for the UK's tech future during US President Donald Trump's state visit to the UK in September last year.

It was also right in the middle of his attempts to get Trump to lift export bans to China of some of the highest performing AI chips, specifically the H200.

An export ban on a less powerful chip had already been lifted. He was, I suggested to him, one of the few people who could walk into the White House to meet Trump, and a few days later meet President Xi Jinping in Beijing.

He made no secret of his views, nor his assessment that he had persuaded Trump of his case.

"President Trump is very clear. He wants America to win and and President Xi wants China to win, and it's possible for both of them too. And the reason for that is because it's not a zero-sum game. The advance of human society is not a zero-sum game."

He is probably the only person in the world that could have spoken that sentence with the authority that he might have heard personally from both these superpower leaders.

However, his view about "zero-sum game" is not backed by many in national security circles.

Their view is that the race to the most advanced forms of AI is entirely zero sum, and requires the West - and the US in particular - to take critical action to hold back Chinese advancement.

The country that creates the most powerful AI systems, from the most powerful chips, will win, in terms of scientific development, of cracking encryption, economic growth and cyber-weapons.

He made a further argument: Far from being a national security challenge, it was, in fact, better for the US that the world "including China" became dependent on US systems, what they called the "American tech stack", with Nvidia chips at its core.

Huang then went even further than that, saying that President Trump "is very clear-eyed" about the idea that "this computing technology is not a national security concern".

He told me "any military is smart enough to build their military on top of their own indigenous technology, and not rely on an adversary to build their technology, build their military capability".

At that time, which is the same moment now being independently investigated over national security concerns and alleged Chinese espionage, Huang was making clear public arguments to lift export bans, and seemed to have a clear idea of President Trump's views.

More than that, he was also disputing the idea that his technology, in China's hands, was any type of national security concern.

Nvidia is the absolute epicentre of the AI tech boom in the US and of the global race for AI supremacy.

Even if the boom turned to bust, Nvidia is still expected to remain in rude health.

It has actual hard revenues of about $400bn this year. Monday's drop of about 4% of its value reflects new and extraordinary risks at this junction of tech and global politics, but the chipmaker is still worth more than $4 trillion.

articles.title: Florida’s red wall is cracking, but Democrats are missing their chance
articles.summary: The midterms exposed the vulnerability of Republican dominance in Florida.
articles.body:
Like many others, when I saw the United States midterm election results on November 4 , I was shocked by the scale of the blue wave that had swept the country, with Democrats and democratic socialists making gains nationwide. Traditionally conservative states, such as South Carolina and Texas, elected Democratic senators for the first time in decades. Georgia also elected its first Black woman as governor.

In an election awash with money from wealthy donors, including tech bosses, Democrats campaigned on affordability, with progressive candidates unapologetically championing working-class interests and Medicare for All. The results suggested a new kind of coalition politics was possible and amounted to a sweeping repudiation of Trump after nearly two years of turmoil: a violent immigration crackdown, conflicts in the Middle East, and threats to Greenland and Canada.

Yet I wondered why Republicans in my home state, Florida, had managed to hold on to a US Senate seat, the governorship and most statewide offices, even as Democrats made historic gains elsewhere.

For most of my childhood, Florida was a swing state with Democratic governors in Tallahassee and mayors in Miami. But by the turn of this century, Republicans had begun to consolidate their hold on state politics. Two factors have helped sustain that dominance: Florida’s long history of voter suppression and support for the Republican Party among conservative Cuban Americans.

Voter suppression has long undermined democracy in the south of the US, especially in my home state. Like other southern states, Florida historically restricted African Americans’ voting rights through literacy tests and poll taxes, which also disenfranchised poor white voters. The Voting Rights Act of 1965 was intended to end these discriminatory practices. Yet in 2000, Florida purged thousands of eligible voters, disproportionately Black, from its rolls. These practices have undermined fair representation and helped skew elections towards Republicans.

Another major factor in the Republican wall is the historically conservative Cuban American vote. Many Cuban Americans, particularly those whose families fled Cuba’s communist government, have traditionally voted Republican. As Trumpism took shape, many found a political home in the MAGA movement. As then-Florida state senator Manny Diaz Jr told the Miami Herald , “If you look at the city of Hialeah [in Miami-Dade], Trump went from winning the city by, like, 100 votes to getting 66 percent of the vote … That’s a growing movement, and it’s not going away.”

Yet despite these longstanding advantages, the 2026 midterms exposed cracks in Republican dominance in Florida. Earlier this year, the Republican-controlled state legislature tried to strengthen its electoral position through gerrymandering, redrawing the boundaries of four Democratic-held congressional districts – the ninth, 14th, 22nd and 25th – to favour Republicans. Governor Ron DeSantis signed the new map into law, but the effort failed to deliver the gains Republicans had hoped for. Democrats Kathy Castor, Pia Dandiya and Jared Moskowitz won in the 14th, 22nd and 25th districts , respectively, while Darren Soto appeared set to retain the ninth.

And the challenge to Republican dominance extended beyond congressional races. Miami-Dade County, which voted for Trump in the 2024 presidential election, backed the Democratic candidates for governor and Senate in 2026. Although Republicans retained both statewide offices, the races were surprisingly close. The Democratic Senate nominee, Angie Nixon, lost by just under three percentage points to Republican incumbent Ashley Moody. David Jolly, the Democratic nominee for governor, lost to Byron Donalds by just 1.3 percentage points, or little more than 100,000 votes.

Even in defeat, Angie Nixon’s campaign was historic. A member of the Democratic Socialists of America who championed the working class, she faced racist attacks from Trump allies and little financial support from the national Democratic establishment. After Nixon won the Democratic Senate primary in August, Laura Loomer, a far-right activist and ally of Donald Trump, posted on X, “Angie Nixon is a ghetto, black, communist.”

When asked whether the Democratic Party would support her grassroots campaign, Nixon recounted a conversation with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer: “He’s going to look into it. That’s what was said, that he’s going to look into it.” Yet neither the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee nor the Senate Majority PAC spent any money supporting her campaign, leaving many wondering whether the Democratic establishment’s failure to invest cost Nixon a winnable Senate seat.

That lack of support is particularly striking given the scale of the national Democratic advance. As the Financial Times reported, the vast majority of districts in the United States swung towards Democrats , delivering a brutal verdict on the MAGA movement, which has felt unstoppable for nearly a decade. If people organise around working-class interests, they can challenge the political power of the ultra-rich. The challenge for Democrats is to back those movements rather than leave them without the resources needed to win.

But election results alone are not enough. People must keep challenging their representatives to improve living conditions, including by revitalising the public sector and expanding universal social programmes. In Florida, the losses did not kill a movement; instead, they have reinvigorated the public’s belief that if people fight, they can win. Angie Nixon is showing us what a democratic socialist fight might look like : “We may have lost this battle, but the war is not over, and I need y’all to stay in this fight. 2028 is around the corner, so Ashley Moody, you better get it right, ’cause we’re coming for you.”

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Red counties with data center projects swung away from GOP in midterms, analysis finds
articles.summary: Humans First's Amy Kremer warns data centers are driving voters away from Republicans as local control and property rights fuel community backlash.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: A new analysis from a conservative AI safety group found that deep-red counties with large data centers or proposed projects shifted further toward Democrats in last week's midterm elections than comparable counties without such projects. Humans First’s analysis, obtained by Fox News Digital, examined public election returns and data-center project records in 1,540 counties across 16 states. The memo used several comparisons to measure what the group describes as a "data center penalty." Across all counties examined, those hosting large data centers shifted an additional 2.2 percentage points toward Democrats compared with non-host counties in the same states. The pattern appeared in 14 of the 16 states and 25 of the 27 governor and Senate races examined. Restricting the analysis to deep-red counties — those President Donald Trump won by at least 20 points in 2024 — produced a 2.1-point raw gap between counties hosting large data centers and comparable counties without projects. Among deep-red counties with projects still in the proposal stage, the gap was 1.1 percentage points after accounting for past voting patterns, rural or urban status, population size, racial and ethnic makeup and recent voting trends. TEA PARTY FOUNDER LAUNCHES NATIONWIDE 'DATA CENTER REVOLT' AGAINST AI DATA CENTER EXPANSION The group identified 114 proposed large data center projects across 92 deep-red counties, potentially setting up more local fights. The memo found that Republican vote totals fell an additional 1.1% in deep-red host counties compared with comparable counties without large data centers, while Democratic vote totals showed no significant change. The memo cautioned that its findings show an association rather than proof that data centers caused voters to change their behavior. County-level results also cannot determine whether Republicans switched their votes or simply stayed home. "Our analysis looked at how counties with data centers voted and how those counties moved to the left," Humans First Chairwoman Amy Kremer told Fox News Digital. "I think this happened for the reason I’ve been warning conservatives and Republicans about for some time: People engage politically when issues affect them personally. There’s nothing more personal than your pocketbook, your health care, your kids and family, your home and your community. A data center involves all of those things, which is why I believe these counties moved away from Republicans," she continued. Humans First’s September "Data Center Revolt" bus tour made 35 stops in 27 states, including 14 stops in the states covered by the analysis. Nine of those stops were in deep-red counties, all of which hosted a large data center project. Those nine counties shifted 2.2 points further toward Democrats after the analysis accounted for its controls, compared with a 0.75-point shift among deep-red host counties overall. The group said those same nine counties showed no comparable gap from 2020 to 2024. The findings do not establish whether the group's visits influenced voting behavior or whether those counties already had stronger opposition to data center development. Separately, voters favored restrictions on data center development or rejected measures supporting such projects in 46 of 47 local data center ballot measures in 2026, according to Ballotpedia. The measures included different types of proposals, including restrictions on development and advisory questions. Kremer said this is a local control issue, stressing that Republicans should focus on protecting property rights and ensuring people have control over how things affect their lives. "Whether you’re talking about AI technology or the infrastructure needed to build AI data centers, the American people have not had a seat at the table," Kremer said. "They haven’t had a say in how the technology affects them or how the data center buildout affects their communities. In many places across the country, developers and companies have gone in and cut deals behind closed doors, under a cloak of darkness, using nondisclosure agreements and shell companies. By the time people in the community find out about the project, it’s too late to stop it." "These projects affect the quality of life and how much money people have. They can increase the cost of electricity and water, while tax abatements are given to trillion-dollar companies — some of the wealthiest companies in the world. That is money coming out of the pockets of the American people," she continued. Kremer added, "When you talk about Iran and gas prices, tariffs and now the AI data center buildout, all of these costs are coming out of people’s pockets. That’s when people engage politically, and I think that’s what we saw last Tuesday." The concerns come amid a broader debate over how data centers should pay for the electricity and grid infrastructure they require. The Energy Department estimates data centers used 4.7% of U.S. electricity in 2024 and, in its reference case, could account for 11.8% by 2030. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission has directed regional grid operators to address safeguards against shifting the costs of serving large electricity users onto other customers. Those developments do not establish that data centers caused higher household rates in the counties examined by Humans First. Tax incentives also vary by state. The National Conference of State Legislatures reported that at least 38 states offer incentives specifically for data centers, including equipment-tax exemptions and, in some states, exemptions involving electricity or property taxes. The Data Center Coalition, an industry trade group, says such incentives are similar to those offered to other capital-intensive industries and argues that data centers generate jobs, investment and tax revenue. Humans First does not support a nationwide or statewide moratorium on data centers, but Kremer said individual communities should be free to approve or reject projects. "Whether you’re talking about pocketbook issues, health care, kids and family, or your home and community, the data center battle is a physical manifestation of all those concerns," she said. "When it comes to the economic impact on their communities, I think data centers absolutely played a role in the election." articles.title: Trump says deportation push hasn’t put 'same pressure' on farmworkers, hotel staff: 'Not even close'
articles.summary: President Donald Trump says his mass deportation push has not targeted waitresses and farmworkers with the same pressure as violent criminals.
articles.body: President Donald Trump said on Monday night that his administration's mass deportation agenda has not put the same pressure on migrant workers as it has on people he described as murderers and drug dealers. During a phone call with C-SPAN, Trump was asked whether law-abiding people who are paying taxes and have lived in the U.S. for a long time should be deported along with migrants who have committed serious offenses. "We certainly haven't put the same push on them as we have on the murderers or the drug dealers," Trump said. "Frankly, a big problem we had is the mental institutions being dumped into our country," he added. "Some very dangerous people were released into our country, to put it mildly. So we have not put the same pressure, obviously. And, you know, we call them the worst of the worst. We haven't put the same pressure on waitresses and on farmworkers, etc. Not even close." TRUMP ADMITS IMMIGRATION ENFORCEMENT MAY HAVE BEEN TOO 'TOUGH' IN FIRST INTERVIEW SINCE MIDTERMS Trump's comments come after he floated the idea of his administration working with Democrats on a deal for some immigrants who have lived illegally in the U.S. for more than a decade after Republicans lost majorities in both chambers of Congress in last week's midterm elections. In a "60 Minutes" interview that aired on Sunday, host Ross Douthat asked Trump whether he was open to working with Democrats on immigration as he enters the lame-duck final stretch of his presidency. "I'd love to do something on immigration," the president replied. When asked whether immigration enforcement hurt Republicans in the midterms, Trump said he believed it both helped and hurt, praising his administration's border enforcement while acknowledging criticism over deportations of people with jobs. "But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs," Trump said. Trump said some Americans believe immigrants who entered the country illegally should be deported, while others believe longtime workers should be allowed to remain, particularly those working in landscaping or hotels and paying taxes. "When you go into a hotel and you have a woman that's working there as a maid, as a cleaner as a this as a that, as a waitress, a lot of good things, great jobs, and all of a sudden they're being taken out of the country, it's tough. It's a tough thing," Trump said, adding that people on the far right want deportations regardless of whether the immigrant living in the country illegally is working. WHITE HOUSE DOUBLES DOWN AFTER TRUMP ANGERS BASE BY FLOATING ILLEGAL ALIEN DEAL WITH DEMS Trump signaled in the interview his willingness to "work a deal" for people who have been in the U.S. illegally for "10 and 15 years." However, Trump said at a White House press briefing earlier on Monday that "there won’t be amnesty" and his policy "hasn’t changed." The president was asked during the phone call with C-SPAN if he expects Republicans to vote against the impeachment of Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth. The House could take up Rep. Thomas Massie's, R-Ky., impeachment resolution against Hegseth as early as Tuesday. Asked what his reaction would be if some Republicans voted for Hegseth's impeachment, Trump said he would be "disappointed." "Maybe we could knock it out fast or we could knock it out over a short, not a long period of time," he said. "Now it's a question of I could do it quickly or not," Trump continued. "The reason I'm doing it this way is because in speaking with Qatar, as you know, the Prime Minister was in the Oval Office today, in speaking to Saudi Arabia, UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait, basically the neighbors who were attacked pretty violently, by the way. But in speaking to them, they'd rather do it this way rather than another hit, which would be approximately five times bigger than the first hit, which basically decimated them. So, I'd like to do it this way, too." Trump added that he believes Iran "would like to make a deal, and we'll find out whether or not that'll happen."

articles.title: Texas governor-elect's plan to freeze electricity prices raises questions over legal authority
articles.summary: Texas Democratic Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa plans to freeze electricity rates on Day One, but experts warn the move could trigger energy shortages.
articles.body: On her first day in office, Texas Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa plans to freeze residential electricity rates in response to what she described as an affordability crisis. "On Day One as governor, I’ll freeze residential electricity rates and make corporations finally pay their fair share," Hinojosa said in an interview with a local energy data group. She reiterated the plan in an interview with the Texas Tribune, stating, "Within an hour of taking the oath of office, I will declare a high-cost emergency in the state of Texas and issue an emergency executive order to … freeze electricity rates." The plan is raising concerns that such a freeze will clash with Texas’ uniquely competitive energy sector, which relies heavily on free-market choice, and that it could inadvertently create energy shortages as suppliers are prevented from adjusting their prices. DEMOCRAT GINA HINOJOSA STUNS ABBOTT, MAKES HISTORY AS FIRST LATINA TEXAS GOVERNOR That’s the concern of Nick Loris, the president of C3 Solutions, a conservative coalition for climate solutions that focuses on energy, environment and agriculture policy. He expects the emergency declaration will face legal challenges almost immediately from energy providers. In particular, he cast doubt on the scope of the emergency declaration. "The Texas Disaster Act lets the governor declare disasters and suspend the regulatory laws and statutes that are in existence. But I think there is a high degree of skepticism, both from courts but also from state policymakers, that this warrants such a claim — and that it is such a disaster," Loris told Fox News Digital. "I would imagine if there were legal challenges, it would come from those affected parties," he added. Loris explained that Texas has fostered one of the most competitive energy environments in the country. In 1999, the state passed Senate Bill 7 — a piece of legislation that opened most of the state to retail choice, allowing customers to pick their preferred retail electric providers (REPs), beginning in 2002. "The legislature finds that the production and sale of electricity is not a monopoly warranting regulation of rates, operations, and services and that the public interest in competitive electric markets requires that, except for transmission and distribution services and for the recovery of stranded costs, electric services and their prices should be determined by customer choices and the normal forces of competition," the Texas Legislature wrote in the law. TEXAS GOV. GREG ABBOTT EFFECTIVELY PAUSES NEW DATA CENTER PROJECTS PENDING STATEWIDE GRID AUDIT As a result of the law, Texas largely operates its own independent energy grid and runs an energy-only wholesale market in which generators are paid primarily for the electricity they produce rather than for standing capacity. Texas has over 100 REPs that energy consumers can pick from, each competing for consumers' business. To Loris, the range of choices provides a remarkable amount of flexibility for consumers. "It's like shopping at a grocery store for cereal for your retail electricity. There's so much choice that you can enter into. Short-term contracts, long-term contracts, use different fuel sources," Loris said. However, he warned that a utilities freeze undermines that competitive environment, causing providers to shoulder the burden of fluctuating supply. "If the electricity suppliers are not covering the costs that they incur, that's going to leave them worse off and make it more vulnerable for them to adequately provide that power," Loris said. They tell people when to speed up, when to slow down, or when to come to a full stop," he added. Having won her Nov. 3 gubernatorial race, Hinojosa will be sworn in on Jan. 19, 2027. articles.title: HUGH HEWITT: Three big legal fights are looming, and Trump needs answers before January
articles.summary: Stephen Miller and the DOJ brace for an epic clash with Congress over executive privilege as Democrats prepare sweeping oversight inquiries.
articles.body: United States Assistant Attorney General T. Elliott Gaiser is going to be a very busy man in 2027. Before the new Congress arrives in January, President Donald Trump should require Gaiser and his team to provide detailed answers to a few very important questions of law. On Friday, November 6, at 3:29 p.m., Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., the incoming chairman of the House Oversight Committee, posted a threat barely disguised as advice directed at new White House chief of staff Stephen Miller: "Steven Miller should lawyer up." At 6:10 p.m. that same day, United States Attorney General Todd Blanche posted a response: "The Chief of Staff already has a lawyer. The Attorney General of the United States and the Department of Justice." ‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH Welcome to the next two years. There is an epic clash coming between the powers of Congress under Article I of the Constitution and the powers of President Trump under Article II. The Supreme Court will referee the clash, but it will start soon, and one of the key participants will be Mr. Gaiser, the assistant attorney general for the Office of Legal Counsel (OLC). OLC is the division of the U.S. Department of Justice that serves as the principal legal adviser to the president and the executive branch. AAG Gaiser was confirmed by the Senate on July 30, 2025. By all accounts, he is a brilliant lawyer. Gaiser helms an office of about two dozen lawyers who are collectively widely regarded as among the top legal minds in the country. The office is a mix of career and political appointees, but all are serious legal scholars. OLC tackles questions President Trump or Attorney General Blanche require it to answer, and it can also supply answers to questions from Cabinet officers and military leaders, as time allows and the president and the AG permit. The Supreme Court does not issue advisory opinions on possible controversies that have not reached it at all or that are premature (cases that are not yet "ripe" for decision), but OLC does. Everyone should expect President Trump to follow the examples of Presidents Clinton, Obama and Biden and play full-court defense against what have already been announced as sweeping inquiries into executive branch conduct. One recent example: On August 10 of this year, OLC opined that "executive privilege can apply to presidential communications with private advisers so long as the communications (1) relate to official presidential decision making, (2) involve or reflect communications with the President or his direct advisers, and (3) are confidential." AG BLANCHE CLASHES WITH ANCHOR ASKING WHETHER IT'S HIS 'JOB' TO DEFEND THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION There is going to be a raft of additional executive privilege questions incoming, as the new Democratic majorities cannot immediately compel testimony about matters over which President Trump has asserted "executive privilege." But there are other pressing questions about "court packing," statehood for the District of Columbia and the constitutionality of the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact that can be asked and answered by OLC before the executive privilege debates begin. Both Republican and Democratic presidents have asserted their privilege in situations that have angered Congress. Sometimes the Supreme Court or the United States Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit has sided with the president, and sometimes it has sided with Congress. TRUMP'S MOVE FROM WILES TO MILLER SIGNALS MAJOR TACTICAL SHIFT FOR GOVERNING WITHOUT CONGRESS President Biden, facing a demand for the audio recordings of his and his ghostwriter’s interviews with special counsel Robert Hur, sought and received an OLC opinion on May 15, 2024, on whether he could assert executive privilege over those recordings. OLC opined that Biden could. Lawsuits were filed challenging that opinion and President Biden’s decision not to release the recordings, and the Trump administration decided to release the recordings. President Clinton asserted a novel Secret Service protective-function privilege as well as a White House attorney-client privilege, both of which were rejected in whole or in material part by the United States Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit. President Obama made claims of executive privilege over materials in the "Fast and Furious" investigation, and when litigation followed, a settlement was reached before a court decision was made. MORNING GLORY: DSA DEMOCRATS' RADICAL PLAN TO RESHAPE AMERICA STARTS WITH THE SUPREME COURT Everyone should expect President Trump to follow the examples of Presidents Clinton, Obama and Biden and play full-court defense against what have already been announced as sweeping inquiries into executive branch conduct by such members as Garcia and Congressman Jamie Raskin, D-Md., who will chair the House Judiciary Committee. Both committees have subpoena powers. President Trump may require a legal opinion from the attorney general under 28 U.S.C. § 511, and when such a demand is made, the AG turns to OLC. Before OLC is deluged with requests from President Trump and AG Blanche in 2027 on the scope of executive privilege across the executive branch, the president could secure some important OLC opinions between now and January 3, when the new Congress is sworn in. Three such questions come to mind in light of last week's sweeping Democratic wins across the country and the often very extreme positions put forward by Democrats campaigning for House or Senate seats. JONATHAN TURLEY: MIDTERMS EMPOWER DEMOCRATS TO TARGET THE ELECTORAL COLLEGE First and perhaps most important: Is it in fact constitutional for Congress to expand the Supreme Court to more than the current nine justices? There is a strong argument that, in the wake of the ratification of the 14th Amendment and the almost immediate passage of the Judiciary Act of 1869 the following April, "court packing" is simply unconstitutional. When Congress set the number of justices at nine in 1869 after expanding it to 10 justices in 1863, and then temporarily reducing it to seven in 1866, Congress and President Grant did so in the shadow of the new Fourteenth Amendment’s guarantee of "due process of law." OLC ought to be tasked by President Trump with weighing in on whether "court packing" violates that guarantee of due process and/or whether packing the court is an unconstitutional attempt to seize control of judicial review, which has always been implicitly vested in the federal courts by the Constitution but which was only made explicit by the Supreme Court in 1803 in the case of Marbury v. Madison, almost a decade and a half after the Constitution was ratified. Democrats also want to make the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico states. The 23rd Amendment to the U.S. Constitution deals with the District of Columbia, and OLC ought to opine on whether statehood for D.C. would require another amendment. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION George Washington University law professor and Fox News contributor Jonathan Turley has already raised another important issue: "With one-party control in states like Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin, the [Democratic] party is ready to get states to join the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact," Turley wrote recently in an op-ed for Fox News. "Under the Compact," Turley explained, "states agree to give all their electoral votes to the presidential ticket that wins the national popular vote." "The constitutionality of the Compact has obviously not been tested," Turley wrote. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP As with "court packing," OLC has never weighed in on either statehood for D.C. or the Compact. AAG Gaiser and his team of big legal brains can study these issues and provide the first comprehensive analysis for the executive branch, including who would have "standing" to bring constitutional challenges to all three schemes and when such challenges would be ripe. Of course, OLC opinions would not bind federal courts, but they would be instrumental in shaping the debate before the courts. Hugh Hewitt is a Fox News contributor and host of "The Hugh Hewitt Show" heard weekday afternoons from 3 PM to 6 PM ET on the Salem Radio Network, and simulcast on Salem News Channel (SNC). Hugh drives Americans home on the East Coast and to lunch on the West Coast on over 400 affiliates nationwide, and on all the streaming platforms where SNC can be seen. He is a frequent guest on the Fox News Channel’s news roundtable, hosted by Bret Baier weekdays at 6pm ET. A son of Ohio and a graduate of Harvard College and the University of Michigan Law School, Hewitt has been a Professor of Law at Chapman University’s Fowler School of Law since 1996 where he teaches Constitutional Law. Hewitt launched his eponymous radio show from Los Angeles in 1990. Hewitt has frequently appeared on every major national news television network, hosted television shows for PBS and MSNBC, written for every major American paper, has authored a dozen books and moderated a score of Republican candidate debates, most recently the November 2023 Republican presidential debate in Miami and four Republican presidential debates in the 2015-16 cycle. Hewitt focuses his radio show and his column on the Constitution, national security, American politics and the Cleveland Browns and Guardians. Hewitt has interviewed tens of thousands of guests, from Democrats Hillary Clinton and John Kerry to Republican Presidents George W. Bush and Donald Trump over his 40 years in broadcasting.
