articles.title: Trump's Supreme Court majority faces looming threat after Dem Senate takeover: 'Stuck'
articles.summary: Justice Samuel Alito confirmed he has no plans to retire, but Democrats' Senate takeover raises stakes for the Supreme Court's conservative majority.
articles.body: Republicans' loss of the U.S. Senate in the midterm elections could have far-reaching consequences for President Donald Trump's judicial agenda, threatening his ability to reshape the federal courts and raising new questions about the future of the Supreme Court's 6-3 conservative majority. With Democrats set to take control of the Senate in January, Republicans face a shrinking window to confirm Trump's judicial nominees, while any future Supreme Court vacancy could leave the president dependent on Democratic support to install a replacement. "Lawless Lawfare" author Alex Swoyer told Fox News Digital the election results could leave the court's oldest conservative justices with a difficult decision over when to retire. "It's likely the justices — mainly Justices Thomas and Alito — are stuck on the high court for at least six more years with Democrats taking control," Swoyer said. "Both in their late 70s, I could see why they may want to retire now, midterm." UNDER-THE-RADAR IMPLICATION OF DEM BLUE WAVE MEANS 'ZERO' CHANCE GOP ACCOMPLISHES CRITICAL GOAL, EXPERTS WARN Justice Clarence Thomas, 78, and Justice Samuel Alito, 76, are the court's two oldest conservatives, making their retirement decisions particularly consequential as Republicans prepare to lose control of the Senate. Alito, however, confirmed to Fox News on Thursday that he has no plans to retire and is committed to serving through at least the current Supreme Court term, with the justices expected to wrap up their major decisions in late June or early July. DEMS SEIZE THE SENATE AS BLUE TIDAL WAVE CRASHES DEEP INTO TRUMP COUNTRY, TOPPLES GOP STRONGHOLDS "While Senate Republicans were able to confirm Justice Barrett in a one-month timeframe in 2020, I don't think this GOP Senate has that same work ethic or ability to push a nominee through ahead of January," Swoyer said. "I think conservatives would like to see them try; however, a judicial nominations expert told me the Senate work calendar ahead of the holidays would not afford them enough time," she added. "While a five-week window seems workable, it doesn't appear like Senate Majority Leader John Thune would have the support to usher such a move at this time." The stakes extend beyond the Supreme Court. As of Nov. 8, the federal judiciary had 28 vacancies, with 16 nominees awaiting confirmation for current and future vacancies, leaving Republicans with limited time to advance Trump's picks before Democrats take control of the Senate. Zack Smith, a senior legal fellow for courts and the Constitution at the Heritage Foundation, said Republicans should focus on confirming Trump's remaining lower-court nominees before their majority expires. CHUCK SCHUMER AFTER SWEEPING DEMOCRATIC MIDTERM VICTORIES: 'I'LL BE RE-ELECTED AS MAJORITY LEADER' "The top priority for Senate Republicans right now should be confirming the lower federal court judges President Trump has already nominated. It will take all senators showing up and doing their part. But it is possible," Smith told Fox News Digital. "As for the Supreme Court, even if a justice announced his or her retirement today, it could prove difficult to get a replacement confirmed before the end of the current Senate, although Senate Republican leadership has indicated a willingness to try. However, neither Justice Alito nor Justice Thomas has indicated any plan to retire." The uncertainty surrounding Thomas and Alito echoes the debate over the late liberal Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, who resisted calls to retire before the 2014 midterms despite concerns that Republicans could take control of the Senate and complicate efforts to confirm an Obama-appointed successor. DEMOCRATIC SENATOR CLAIMS GOP 'STOLE' TWO SCOTUS SEATS IN 2016, 2020, CALLS FOR EXPANSION Republicans won the Senate in 2014 and, two years later, refused to consider Obama's Supreme Court nominee, Merrick Garland, following Justice Antonin Scalia's death. Trump won the 2016 election and appointed Neil Gorsuch to Scalia's seat in 2017. Ginsburg remained on the bench until her death in September 2020, just weeks before the presidential election. Trump nominated Amy Coney Barrett to replace her, and the Republican-controlled Senate confirmed Barrett days before Election Day. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Barrett's confirmation gave conservatives a 6-3 majority on the Supreme Court, a balance that has shaped some of the nation's most consequential legal decisions, including the 2022 ruling overturning Roe v. Wade.

articles.title: Republicans, reeling from an election drubbing, will choose their leadership in Congress
articles.summary: Reps. Jim Jordan and Steve Scalise are vying for the top spot in the House, while John Thune is expected to remain Senate Republican leader, despite a conservative push to delay.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — After a blue tidal wave swept them from power, House and Senate Republicans will try to pick up the pieces Tuesday and select their leadership teams for the new Congress. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., has already heeded his party’s call for new blood, announcing he will forgo a bid for minority leader and step down from leadership. But other GOP leaders in both chambers are fighting to hang on to power in the wake of last week’s historic midterm drubbing. The House: Scalise vs. Jordan In the House, Johnson’s decision has triggered a two-person race for minority leader. Johnson’s trusted top lieutenant and fellow Louisiana Republican, Majority Leader Steve Scalise, is fending off a challenge from Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan of Ohio, the founding chairman of the hard-right House Freedom Caucus. Both are allies of President Donald Trump and ran unsuccessfully for speaker in 2023 after Kevin McCarthy was ousted. The elections will be held behind closed doors and by secret ballot. Candidates will make their pitches to the conference beginning at 9 a.m. ET, with a vote in the afternoon. Scalise made the pitch to colleagues that he can unify factions of House Republicans against the “socialists” coming to Washington, while Jordan, a former Oversight Committee chairman, argued that he’s best positioned to combat Democratic investigations of the Trump administration and its allies, telling colleagues he’s “battle-tested on the oversight front and I know the Democrats’ playbook.” Either will need a majority of the conference to vote for him to secure the job. Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., is seeking the whip job, the party’s top vote counter and the No. 2 post in the minority. But he faces an insurgent challenge from August Pfluger of Texas, the chairman of the Republican Study Committee, the largest caucus of conservatives on Capitol Hill. And House GOP Conference Chair Lisa McClain of Michigan is trying to beat back challenges from two colleagues: Erin Houchin of Indiana, who holds a lower-level leadership post, and Greg Steube of Florida, who berated the current leadership team for choosing “accommodation over conviction.” “We’re ready to move on. We need a pivot,” a House GOP lawmaker who is backing Jordan over Scalise told NBC News on the condition of anonymity to speak frankly about the rival candidates. “Everything is on the table” after the Democratic landslide, the lawmaker said. The Senate: Thune faces grumbling Senate Republicans also are poised to hold a closed-door vote Tuesday to pick their leaders. Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota is running for minority leader, and so far nobody has announced plans to oppose him. But a small group of Senate Republicans has sought to delay the elections, saying the party needs more time to process the election results. “A week ago, we had the worst election result in decades. We need a discussion about what went wrong, how we fix it, what we stand for, and how our agenda must focus on the concerns of the American people,” Sen. David McCormick, R-Pa., said in a statement. “As I’ve shared with Leader Thune, I don’t believe we should move to leadership elections until we have digested and debated the lessons of the midterms and how to move forward,” he said. “We need leadership in place fast, but Tuesday is too soon.” Five other Senate Republicans, led by Budget Committee Chairman Ron Johnson of Wisconsin, sent a letter to Senate Republican Conference Chairman Tom Cotton of Arkansas asking for “a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead” before the elections are held Tuesday morning. As in the House, senators’ votes are cast by secret ballot, and candidates require a simple majority of the conference to win. Apart from Thune, Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso of Wyoming and Cotton are expected to win their races to stay on as the second-ranked and third-ranked Republicans in the next Congress. Jeffries and Schumer favorites to lead Dems After last week’s Democratic rout, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, both New York Democrats, are favorites to be the next House speaker and Senate majority leader. But they, too, face grumbling from rank-and-file members. No one has emerged to challenge either for the top jobs, though Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., opened the door Monday to potentially running for majority leader amid a push from the grassroots to find an alternative to Schumer. A person familiar with Van Hollen’s thinking told NBC News on Monday: “The senator has received an outpouring of calls on running for majority leader and is now in active listening mode. The door is not shut.” Democrats at the Senate’s new-member orientation Monday said the question of their leadership team hasn’t come up in private conversations. “Most of us are just trying to figure out where our office is and how to find the bathroom,” said Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan, D-Minn. “It’s really exciting to be here and to meet a lot of my colleagues who’ve been campaigning. I know how hard we’ve been working. And to be here together — it’s really exciting.” As for Van Hollen’s potentially running for majority leader, Flanagan said she is “certainly open to new leadership” but is “not ready to make any commitments at this point.” Senate Democrats will elect their leadership team in a private meeting in early December, while House Democrats will pick their team next week. Several progressives have said they are undecided about whether to back Jeffries for speaker as grassroots groups urge the party to more aggressively confront Trump and enact progressive policies. “We’re not withholding votes. What we’re doing [is] saying we’re undecided,” said Rep.-elect Adam Hamawy, D-N.J. “We want to sit and have a conversation about the issues and what’s the plan going forward.” But Jeffries has such a large majority — NBC News projects Democrats will secure 259 seats — that he can afford roughly 40 defections and still win the 218 votes needed to become speaker on the House floor on Jan. 3. “We’re going to work as hard as we can to get to the 218 number, and we’re confident that we will get to that number and beyond,” Jeffries told reporters when he was asked about disgruntled progressives. Jeffries and his top lieutenants, Katherine Clark of Massachusetts, Pete Aguilar of California and Ted Lieu of California, are so far running unopposed for the top four leadership posts: speaker, majority leader, majority whip and Democratic Caucus chair.

articles.title: GOP senator withholds support for Thune as leadership showdown looms
articles.summary: Rick Scott says he won't back John Thune for Senate GOP leader without a specific plan for the lame duck session before Democrats take control.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: A Senate Republican isn’t ready to support Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., to stay as the top Republican as the GOP’s leadership elections fast approach. Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., in an interview with Fox News Digital, argued that whoever would be the next to lead the Senate GOP and earn his vote in the process needed to lay out a plan on how Republicans would pass key agenda items heading into the lame-duck session of Congress before Senate Democrats take control in January. Thune plans to run again for another term as the GOP leader, but Scott and a cohort of others want to delay Tuesday morning’s leadership elections to debrief after stunning losses across the board on Election Night. Whether he’ll support Thune for another term depends on his pitch. SENATE GOP REBELS MOVE TO DELAY LEADERSHIP VOTE, DEMAND RECKONING AFTER MIDTERM DISASTER "I don't want to put the cart before the horse," Scott said. "I mean, I think the first step is what do we want to accomplish? And then anybody, including John Thune, if they want to be that, the first thing I have to say is, ‘Do they want to do that?’" "If that's not what they want to accomplish, then why would we elect them? But if that's what they want to accomplish, then tell us why they're the best at it," he continued. Senate Democrats flipped the upper chamber with wins in red states across the country, clinching a 54-seat majority that could grow even more depending on the outcomes of outstanding races in Mississippi and Alaska. STATE OF PLAY: BLUE WAVE SWEEPS DEMOCRATS INTO POWER, WITH KEY RACES STILL HANGING IN BALANCE That gives Republicans little time with a trifecta in government to ram through key remaining agenda items before Democrats officially take over. Thune still plans on running for leader, too, despite the grumbling among Republicans. He said on Monday after lawmakers returned to Washington that he expected a "very engaged conversation" ahead of the leadership election. "We'll see where it goes from there, but, yeah, I'm running for leader, and I think it's important that we have that discussion, and we will," Thune said. Scott said that he wants the candidates to be "specific" on how they can balance the budget and pass a slew of legislation, including a stock trading ban for lawmakers, permitting reform, the National Defense Authorization Act and the SAVE America Act. SCHUMER TANKS POPULAR INSIDER TRADING BAN IN DEM EFFORT TO DERAIL REPUBLICAN'S AGENDA AHEAD OF MIDTERMS All of that, he said, would be a show that Republicans are listening to voters after getting pummeled in the midterms. "Back home, they don't care about anything other than do we make their lives better," Scott said. Thune is so far running unopposed for the top job — Scott reiterated that he had no interest in running again, trying twice for the gig, once against Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., in 2022, and in 2024 when Senate Republicans were searching for McConnell’s replacement. When asked if he would like to see someone else jump into the fray, Scott said, "Oh, I wouldn't do that to anybody." Scott and Sens. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., Ted Budd, R-N.C., John Kennedy, R-La., and Mike Lee, R-Utah, all signed onto a letter demanding that Republicans meet before holding their leadership elections and delay voting until they have a full debrief on the midterm losses and what comes next. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP They’re joined by Sens. Jim Banks, R-Ind., and Dave McCormick, R-Pa., who called for the elections to be delayed but did not sign onto the letter pushing leadership for a meeting. When asked how long he’d like to see the leadership elections delayed, Scott said, "I think this first step is how long is it gonna take us to agree on what our path should be?" "If we can get that done quickly, then we can, you know, have elections after that," he said. "And then people that want to run with that agenda in mind, saying they believe in that agenda and will work hard to get that agenda accomplished, then that's how we would decide how we vote."

articles.title: Withered MAGA coalition opened door to Democratic wave
articles.summary: We can certainly say that Vice President Vance has a point about voters who backed President Trump in 2024 switching sides and voting Democratic in last week’s midterm elections. Exit polls suggest that 7 percent of Trump voters did indeed back Democrats in federal races this year. That’s not “a lot,” which is how the…
articles.body:
We can certainly say that Vice President Vance has a point about voters who backed President Trump in 2024 switching sides and voting Democratic in last week’s midterm elections. Exit polls suggest that 7 percent of Trump voters did indeed back Democrats in federal races this year. That’s not “a lot,” which is how the vice president described the red-to-blue cohort, but it’s not nothing.

It is, however, only about half of the share of voters in 2010 who had voted for former President Obama in 2008 and then voted Republican in the midterms. It’s also a little less than the 10 percent of switchers in Obama’s second midterm in 2014. Seven percent just happens to be exactly the same share of voters who backed former President Biden in 2020 and then switched to vote Republican in 2022. So, there’s no evidence of some major revolt among Republicans.

It is, though, perhaps an appealing thought for Trump and his vice president to believe that, as Vance said, “Our voters are turning out, but they may not vote for us.” It is a more appetizing story for the administration to think that their voters weren’t dropouts but were present and actively punishing the GOP for the Iran war and the U.S. alliance with Israel.

There’s no doubt that a big chunk of the electorate wanted some disengagement with Israel: 51 percent said America did too much to support Israel, while the other 49 percent were either for the status quo (37 percent) or actually increasing support (12 percent). It’s also true that the war is unpopular: 63 percent said attacking Iran was the wrong decision.

But that doesn’t mean Republicans had a big problem with turncoat voters. It just means that there weren’t enough Republican voters, period. In this year’s electorate, 49 percent of voters said they had voted for then-Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024, but only 44 percent had voted for Trump. And of the 4 percent of this year’s electorate that hadn’t voted in 2024, 70 percent chose Democrats for federal office.

These are only exit polls, so it should all be taken with a handful of salt, but it certainly does point us toward a picture of the electorate that describes what happened to Republicans last week. Democrats were highly mobilized, independent voters went almost 60 percent for the blue team and a lot of Republicans just stayed home. We knew about the blue wave but wondered if the red wall could be formed in time to withstand the blow. It turns out that it could not.

Specific states and districts may depart from what happened in the nation as a whole. Texas stands out for several reasons, including the state’s large number of Hispanic voters (who returned to their pre-2024 low levels of GOP support) and younger voters (with whom Republicans dropped to Obama-era lows, losing voters under 30 by almost 50 points).

Texas may better answer Vance’s description just given the magnitude of the beating Republicans took there, as the party was shut out of every statewide office in an election for the first time since the 1980s.

High prices were most certainly a factor, but one wonders how much the magnitude of that thumping had to do with Iran and Israel, and how much was the result of the GOP going all in on the Senate candidacy of Texas state Attorney General Ken Paxton, a candidate so deficient that the president found himself begging voters to support him, even though he is hard to like. If they have to get your estranged wife to cut a campaign ad saying that Republicans should vote a straight ticket despiteyou being on the ballot, you know you’re not in a good place.

So, yes, given how Republican Texas is, we can safely say that a significant number of Republicans backed the blue this year. We can say the same thing about Kansas and South Carolina, both very Republican states. There just aren’t enough Democrats and independents in those places to fuel victories. And in both cases, the story was also candidate quality. GOP Sens. Darline Graham (S.C.) and Roger Marshall (Kan.) were not bad candidates in the way that Paxton was a bad candidate, but they surely were not good. Marshall and Graham had both hung their political identities on their attachment to and influence with Trump. With Trump less popular than ever, even in places where he remains above water with voters, that was no adequate bulwark.

In Kansas, a not insignificant number of Hispanic voters helped do Marshall in. But in South Carolina, as it was in much of the South, Black turnout overflowed the banks of every river. If Mississippi’s Senate race comes in for Democrats, as it looks likely that it will, we will tell a similar story there: Republicans had a weak nominee, their voters dropped out and Black voters tuned in.

The story in the South and other very red places, is that the national climate created a generational opportunity for highly mobilized Democrats to score victories that would have been unthinkable a year ago. And, in the races where the Republicans put up particularly weak candidates, Democrats rang the bell.

But the overall story of the electorate told by the 2026 exit poll is pretty straightforward: Independents turned decisively against a Republican Party they had given about half of their support to two years ago. When the most persuadable chunk of the electorate gives a party just 33 percent of the vote, the verdict is pretty clear. Add in the exuberance of Democrats and the droopy Republicans and you have the typical ingredients of a midterm rout, just with the volume turned up to 11.

It would be comforting for the Republican establishment to think that this can be fixed by dumping Israel or a truce with Iran, because that would mean that their coalition was durable and reliable but only needed to be accommodated. The truth is that this rising tide sank all boats moored in MAGA’s harbor.

articles.title: John Thune’s leadership bid collides with conservative demands for lame-duck agenda
articles.summary: Senate GOP conservatives are threatening to postpone and possibly derail Sen. John Thune’s (S.D.) bid to serve another term as Senate Republican leader, seeking leverage over how Thune manages a lame-duck session that represents a final chance to pass President Trump’s priorities through a Republican-controlled Congress. Senate conservatives led by Sens. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.), Mike…
articles.body:
Senate GOP conservatives are threatening to postpone and possibly derail Sen. John Thune’s (S.D.) bid to serve another term as Senate Republican leader, seeking leverage over how Thune manages a lame-duck session that represents a final chance to pass President Trump’s priorities through a Republican-controlled Congress.

Senate conservatives led by Sens. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.), Mike Lee (R-Utah) and Rick Scott (R-Fla.) are pushing to postpone Tuesday’s scheduled election of the Senate Republican leadership slate, which is headed by Thune, to have “a robust discussion” about what went wrong in last week’s election.

They’re arguing Thune’s leadership needs to be further evaluated and that how aggressively he manages the next two months of the Senate’s calendar should be weighed as part of any decision to reelect him to another two years as Republican leader.

The Senate conservatives are pressing for a more thorough evaluation of their leaders a few days after Trump lashed out at the Senate for “getting nothing passed.”

But Thune and his allies are pushing back against delaying the leadership election, which would give his critics in the conference more time to take potshots at leadership decisions.

Thune told reporters Monday he’ll listen to his colleagues’ demands for delaying the election but indicated he doesn’t see a need to do so.

“I’m open to hearing what the arguments are for that. I don’t know that that solves anything,” he said. “It’s going to be a decision that’s ultimately made by Republican senators.”

Sen. John Hoeven (R-N.D.), an influential member of the Senate Appropriations Committee and close Thune ally, predicted the leadership election would take place on Tuesday as scheduled.

“I think we will” vote on Tuesday, Hoeven said. “I’m fine. I’m going to support Sen. Thune, and I think it makes sense to go ahead.”

Hoeven said unless there’s a bombshell disclosure made at the meeting, it would make sense to get the leadership team in place before the lame-duck session begins.

He, however, said conservatives who want to make recommendations about how Thune and his leadership team could improve their performance should be given ample time to air their suggestions and gripes.

“It’s about having a discussion on the front end. I think we’ll have that discussion. And for folks that want to talk, we’ll let them talk as long as they want,” he said. “If somebody has something they want to say, you got to” let them talk.

“You might have heard it before,” he quipped, noting calls from conservatives for leaders to adopt a more “collaborative” style have been made many times before.

Lee, a staunch Trump ally, argued GOP colleagues should have a chance to assess how Thune and the rest of the GOP leadership team use the remaining weeks of the Senate and House Republican majorities before voting for a new leadership slate.

“Perhaps Senate Republicans should assess leadership candidates based on how they lead the conference over the next few weeks while we still have the majority—especially while the full membership of the next conference is still being determined,” he posted on the social platform X, noting the results of the Alaska and Mississippi Senate races have yet to be determined.

Johnson and other conservatives are pushing hard for Thune to advance a third budget reconciliation package in the lame-duck Congress to fund the Pentagon and fulfill the White House’s June request for emergency defense funding to help replenish weapons and munitions stockpiles depleted by the Iran war.

Some conservatives are also pressing for a last-ditch attempt to pass the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE America) Act, which would require people registering to vote to show documented proof of citizenship and voters to show photo identification when casting ballots.

Scott, the chair of the Senate Steering Committee, on Sunday called for every candidate running for a Senate Republican leadership position to commit to passing it in the lame-duck session.

“I’ve been fighting for over two years to get the SAVE/SAVE America Act passed in the Senate. We have two months to get it done. Every candidate for a leadership job must commit to passing it. Failure is not an option,” he said on X.

Conservatives are demanding their leaders cancel the weeklong Thanksgiving recess to keep senators in Washington to pass what remains of Trump’s agenda through budget reconciliation, which would allow them to circumvent a Democratic filibuster.

“The Senate should be working 24/7 to get our agenda done. NO EXCUSES,” Scott posted on social media.

Thune, however, warned a drawn-out debate on the SAVE America Act, which has already received multiple votes on the Senate floor and failed to advance this year, or a time-consuming debate over another budget resolution could crowd out other Trump priorities.

He indicated he wants to prioritize confirming as many of Trump’s judicial and executive branch nominees before turning control of the Senate over to Democrats.

“If you look at what we have to get done in the lame duck — and I had this conversation with the president a couple of days ago — a lot of it’s going to revolve around getting the judges across the finish line,” Thune said.

“There’s a number of them that we’ve got that will be available for consideration on the Senate floor, both District Court and circuit. And then a whole lot of executive branch noms, too, that I think the administration would like to get cleared,” Thune.

Senate Republicans anticipate they’ll need to confirm 19 District Court-level judicial nominees and 4 circuit-level judicial nominees to clear the decks before Democrats take over.

They want to confirm more than 100 executive branch nominees, though they can be moved as a package. Judicial nominees could not be included in such a package.

The GOP leader pointed out Republicans and Democrats need to reach a short-term government funding deal by Dec. 11 to avoid another shutdown.

He said he’s open to moving a third budget reconciliation package but questioned whether the votes would be there to move it.

Several Republicans on the Appropriations Committee have expressed their opposition to circumventing the regular congressional spending process and funding the Defense Department through a budget reconciliation package.

“If there is a path forward on reconciliation, I’m open to that. I’ve said that all along,” Thune said. “Something like that probably ends up originating in the House. We’ll see if there’s a political appetite to do it.”

He emphasized budget reconciliation “takes a lot of time.”

“Right now the priority is going to be getting the judges across the finish line,” he said.

articles.title: House Republicans face leadership reckoning after midterm bloodbath
articles.summary: House Republicans are preparing to elect a new leadership team that will face the challenge of steering the conference through its transition to the minority after the party’s huge midterm losses last week. A growing number of Republicans have argued the losses exposed shortcomings in leadership and messaging, fueling calls for a shake-up. The contests…
articles.body:
House Republicans are preparing to elect a new leadership team that will face the challenge of steering the conference through its transition to the minority after the party’s huge midterm losses last week.

A growing number of Republicans have argued the losses exposed shortcomings in leadership and messaging, fueling calls for a shake-up.

The contests are already taking shape, with House Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan (Ohio) challenging House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (La.) for minority leader. Republican Study Committee Chair August Pfluger (Texas) is going head-to-head against House GOP Whip Tom Emmer (Minn.), while Republican Reps. Greg Steube (Fla.) and Erin Houchin (Ind.) are challenging GOP Conference Chair Lisa McClain (Mich.).

But the stakes extend beyond the immediate leadership battles: The decisions Republicans make could shape the party’s direction, its strategy for rebuilding and its ability to reclaim the House majority in 2028.

“Republican leaders repeatedly told Americans the economy was doing just fine, even as the cost of housing, groceries, and everyday necessities continued to strain family budgets. When the median home costs six times the median household income, telling people everything is affordable if you just work harder is insulting. Gaslighting did not lower the cost of gas, homes, or healthcare,” Rep. Warren Davidson (R-Ohio) wrote on social media last week.

“Speaker Johnson accepted some responsibility with dignity and swiftly stepped aside. I respect his example. We cannot expect different results from the same leaders,” Davidson added.

Republicans are slated to hold their leadership elections Tuesday.

President Trump told reporters he will stay out of the minority leader contest. While Trump has traditionally wielded considerable influence over House Republicans, several candidates he endorsed lost their races last week.

Scalise has sought to cast himself as an experienced hand who can unite the conference, pointing to his longstanding efforts to bring members together, build consensus and deliver on his commitments in his “Dear Colleague” letter.

“Steve is the right guy for the job. Plain and simple. He’s a tried and tested leader, who has the experience to lead House Republicans for the next two years, and the chops to reclaim the majority in 2028,” a GOP member, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, told The Hill last week.

Jordan, meanwhile, argued in his letter to colleagues that for too long, Republicans have “operated without a clear plan to survive the hour or the day in front of us.” Jordan is a co-founder of the far-right House Freedom Caucus and has risen to prominence as chair of the Judiciary Committee launching investigations into Trump’s political opponents.

The match-up will likely reignite old tensions. Scalise initially won the Republican nomination to be Speaker in 2023, beating Jordan in a secret ballot vote. But he withdrew from the race when it became clear he would not win enough support from his conference to get the votes needed on the House floor. Jordan was later chosen as the nominee for Speaker, but he repeatedly fell short of the votes needed to secure the gavel.

“I think we’re going into a wartime situation where we are going to be the rebel alliance, and we’re going to need someone who knows how to fight, and Jim Jordan knows how to do that,” a second GOP lawmaker told The Hill.

A similar divide is unfolding in the races for minority whip and GOP conference chair, with incumbents touting their records and challengers making the case that a fresh face is needed to help the party regain its footing and win back voters.

“If we learned two things in this last week about Republican messaging, the first is that our message was meaningless. That’s evidence in the massive losses we took across the country on Tuesday. But the other messaging thing that we learned was that the messaging from the American people was loud and clear that they’re looking for something different, so we have to do better for our constituents and our members,” Houchin said Sunday on Fox News.

Houchin also took a shot at McClain, arguing in the Fox News interview that if the GOP conference chair was the job “she wanted to do, that’s the job that she should have done when she had the opportunity.”

McClain touted endorsements from more than a dozen of her colleagues on social media last week, writing that she’s “ready to fight for every member, challenge every Democratic attack, and hold them accountable for every reckless decision.”

Johnson declined to weigh in on the leadership elections. The Hill reached out to Johnson’s office for comment.

House Ways and Means Committee Chair Jason Smith (R-Mo.), meanwhile, has called for the leadership elections to be delayed.

“We are less than a week removed from Tuesday’s elections, and need to understand how and why we lost the trust of the American people,” he wrote on social media Monday. “We also need, as a Conference, to address how our rules have empowered members to vote against rules, bills, and even the Speaker. Failing to address these issues before choosing someone new to lead our Conference is doing a disservice to whoever we choose as Republican Leader.”

articles.title: The Memo: Trump’s mixed signals give way to a doubling down after midterms defeat
articles.summary: President Trump has been sending conflicting signals as he grapples with the comprehensive defeat suffered by his Republican Party in the midterm elections. But a day or two of ambiguity seems to be giving way to a doubling down of his usual, hypercombative approach. Trump acknowledged in a CBS “60 Minutes” interview broadcast on Sunday…
articles.body:
President Trump has been sending conflicting signals as he grapples with the comprehensive defeat suffered by his Republican Party in the midterm elections.

But a day or two of ambiguity seems to be giving way to a doubling down of his usual, hypercombative approach.

Trump acknowledged in a CBS “60 Minutes” interview broadcast on Sunday that some of his immigration enforcement actions had been seen as “too tough.”

But he has promoted the chief architect of those policies, Stephen Miller, to be his new White House chief of staff. And at a hastily arranged media briefing at the White House late on Monday afternoon, Trump seemed to walk back his apparent admission of excessive enforcement.

“We have a very strong deportation policy,” Trump insisted. “My policy hasn’t changed.”

In the “60 Minutes” interview, Trump claimed he could curb his penchant for insulting Democrats to work with them.

But moments later, he said he would never forgive foes like former FBI Director James Comey and Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.).

“I do hate some of my enemies, and I always will,” he said.

On the global stage, it’s not at all clear what Trump is planning as his next steps in the war on Iran. His remarks on this at the Monday afternoon briefing were, once again, inexact.

Meanwhile, after initially saying that he accepted the results of the elections, the president began ventilating unsupported allegations of malfeasance on Monday, writing on social media, “Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong???”

To critics of the president, it’s quite plain what is going on. They see him as merely paying brief lip service to the idea that he might be conciliatory, when his intention is to pursue rigidly hard-line policies.

“It’s just so telling once again that Trump has never actually cared about the Republican Party,” said Olivia Troye, an aide to then-Vice President Mike Pence during the first Trump administration who has become a vigorous critic of the president.

“It’s very striking that his takeaway is to double down on an agenda that is clearly unpopular with the American people, especially as is signaled by putting Stephen Miller at the helm.”

Trump loyalists see things entirely differently. They contend that Trump is preparing for battle with a Democratic Congress that has already telegraphed its intention to go after the president and his allies.

Joe DiGenova, the former U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia who recently resigned from his role investigating a supposed “grand conspiracy” against Trump, said he continues to support the president “wholeheartedly.”

“I think Stephen Miller is a very bright guy, very smart, and any president should have the chief of staff that he wants. This is clearly the chief of staff that the president wants,” DiGenova said.

DiGenova placed the blame for the GOP’s midterm defeat on two factors — a GOP Congress that he said had been unwilling to pass legislation that the MAGA base wanted, including the SAVE America Act, and a misplaced confidence that negotiations with Iran could reach a satisfactory conclusion.

But he also contended the choices now facing Trump — between sticking with his agenda and accommodating himself to life with a Democratic Congress — were not mutually exclusive.

“I think you go full-bore ahead while trimming your sails,” he said. “He is not going to be dealing with a Republican Congress, so he doesn’t have any choice. He will be a veto president for the next two years.”

Democrats, fresh off their victory, want to press their gains — including in the area of accountability.

Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), the incoming chair of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, wrote simply “lawyer up” on social media on election night.

On the topic of the Miller appointment, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) — who is likely soon to become Speaker — told reporters Monday, “Stephen Miller is a stone-cold racist. His track record speaks for itself, and I’ve got zero interest in working with that kind of individual.”

Few Republicans have publicly criticized the appointment of Miller, but one exception came from Rep. Marlin Stutzman (R-Ind.).

“I think that the decision to elect Stephen Miller is a mistake. He’s not liked out here in the Midwest by people, they don’t like his tone,” Stutzman told CNN’s “Inside Politics” on Sunday.

Others in the broader Republican world are, at least for the moment, taking a philosophical view, basically accepting that Trump is Trump, and always will be.

“He’s 80 years old, and that isn’t when people generally reinvent themselves,” GOP strategist Alex Conant drily noted.

Conant contended that the midterm loss couldn’t be pinned on one factor, so a remedy was not necessarily easy to come by.

“When you lose by that magnitude, there are lots of things that contribute to it,” Conant said

“This was a referendum on Donald Trump, and he is not very popular right now. It’s a reflection that inflation is still too high, there is an unpopular war [and] corruption showed up as a concern in the exit polls. I think people with agendas tried to make the election about their one thing, but the truth is, it was many things.”

For some Republicans, the best approach right now seems to be to batten down the hatches and hope that Democrats overreach.

Republican strategist Brad Blakeman, whose brother Bruce lost his gubernatorial bid in New York to incumbent Gov. Kathy Hochul (D), noted there was a whole range of adverse factors for the GOP that “took its toll.”

But, Blakeman insisted, “the Democrats have not got the lesson the American people delivered. It’s not division, it’s not getting even — it’s governing. And I haven’t heard, yet, anybody speaking to governing.”

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

articles.title: Democrats see a path back in Florida. Now they must convince the party
articles.summary: Florida is one of the few places in the country where the blue wave that swept the country appeared to crash into a brick wall on Election Night. The state is once again a punchline, the subject of mocking memes and jokes on social media after failing to also capitalize on the overwhelming nationwide wins. …
articles.body:
Florida is one of the few places in the country where the blue wave that swept the country appeared to crash into a brick wall on Election Night.

The state is once again a punchline, the subject of mocking memes and jokes on social media after failing to also capitalize on the overwhelming nationwide wins .

But Florida Democratic Party chair Nikki Fried is taking somewhat of a victory lap anyway — using the midterm election results to make the case to national Democratic operatives and donors that the party is closer to breaking through than many believe.

While David Jolly, Florida’s Democratic gubernatorial candidate, fell short , as did Senate candidate Angie Nixon, Fried said the results proved they’re not far from adding shades of purple to Florida’s crimson hue.

Talks with Democrats have been very consistent: “Yes we could win. … Imagine if we put a little more into Florida,” Fried said in an interview with The Hill, recounting her conversations with operatives in recent days.

Fried pointed to the fact that Democrats made considerable progress this election cycle, even if the statewide elections went sideways. She noted Democrats flipped 16 Republican-held state House seats and another in the state Senate. The party also broke the Republican supermajority in the Florida House, and Democratic candidates are on track to hold on to the four congressional seats redistricted to favor the GOP.

Florida Democrats, Fried said, “created all of this by our sheer grit.”

The state’s political transformation over the past decade has been striking. In the early aughts, it was one of the key presidential battlegrounds. On election night in 2000, Tim Russert, NBC’s “Meet the Press” moderator at the time, famously took to a small white board to declare the presidential race would come down to “Florida, Florida, Florida.”

But the Sunshine State has morphed from purple to red over the years. In 2020, Democrats held a narrow advantage of roughly 97,000 registered voters. Six years later, Republicans outnumbered them by more than 1.5 million.

Since then, Democrats have been feverishly trying to fight back — and have made some progress.

The party has highlighted an 8 percent increase in Democratic voter turnout from the 2020 election to the 2024 election. And the state party has done work to make gains on school boards and county commissions. Perhaps the biggest moment in recent years occurred when Miami-Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava won reelection by a wide margin in 2024.

This spring, Democrats also notably flipped two state House seats in a pair of special elections, including the district where President Trump’s Mar-a-Lago is located.

Those inroads were on full display last week when Miami-Dade County — a onetime blue stronghold that President Trump carried by more than 11 percentage points — swung back toward Democrats. Jolly, for example, carried the county by about 7 points over Republican Gov.-elect Byron Donalds. Nixon also won the county, defeating Republican Sen. Ashley Moody by nearly 56,000 votes.

Statewide, Jolly lost by about 1 point while Moody bested Nixon by almost 3 points.

Fernand Amandi, who served as a senior adviser on the Jolly campaign, said he was gutted by Tuesday’s results, mostly because he viewed the race as winnable if there had been a little more investment from the party apparatus.

“Florida is not Utah, Wyoming or Montana. We’ve shown — even this century — that it can be won, but it requires a permanent campaign infrastructure,” Amandi said. “Democrats have ceded Florida, and they’re going to continue paying the price if they don’t engage in earnest.”

“The message for national Democrats when it comes to Florida is invest or die,” Amandi said. “Unfortunately, Florida is going to keep biting them in the ass because this is the lab for MAGA.”

Matt Bennett, the senior vice president for public affairs and co-founder of Third Way, a center-left think tank, said candidate quality, particularly in the Sunshine State’s Senate race, would have helped the state. Nixon, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), pulled off a major upset over moderate Alex Vindman this summer to clinch the Democratic nomination.

“Angie Nixon was a uniquely bad candidate,” Bennett said. “She joined the DSA … and it’s tough to think of a worse thing to do. Socialism is not popular in Florida.”

Nixon, for her part, outperformed Democrats who ran for Senate in the last two cycles. The closest race in recent memory was in 2018, when then-Sen. Bill Nelson lost by less than 1 point to now-Sen. Rick Scott (R). Republicans won by double digits in the 2022 and 2024 Senate contests.

Bennett’s think tank put out a postelection analysis showing that moderate Senate candidates flipped six Republican-held seats and successfully defended another seat in Georgia. Those results outperformed former Vice President Kamala Harris’s 2024 margins in those states by an average of 21 percentage points.

“It’s pretty evident that good moderate candidates do better in states like Florida,” Bennett said, quipping that Election Day was like an adoption agency, and Florida was the lone orphan left behind.

Democratic strategist Steve Schale, who is based in the Sunshine State and headed up former President Obama’s presidential operation in Florida, agreed with Bennett. In addition to driving out base voters, Schale said, “you have to be able to win crossover voters.”

Still, Schale argued that Democrats made considerable progress last week.

“If you had told me before the election that Democrats would make significant gains in the Florida House, and they were going to win every seat that was redrawn, I would have said, ‘That’s a really good f‑‑‑ing year,'” he added.

Amandi, however, said national Democrats are “going to live with regret about what could have been” this cycle.

Florida, he said, is a “Republican sanctuary fortress until Democrats can prove otherwise.”

articles.title: Reporter’s Notebook: House leadership up for grabs as GOP reckons with devastating losses
articles.summary: Thomas Massie is reintroducing articles of impeachment against Pete Hegseth, and the math suggests House Republicans may not be able to stop it.
articles.body: Internal House and Senate party leadership elections are some of the most fascinating exercises to unfold on Capitol Hill. Both House and Senate Democrats and House and Senate Republicans will choose their leaders in the coming days. And the changes are going to be seismic. But not everyone is on board with heir apparent leaders. That’s what makes this process so intriguing. However, there are only two rules in leadership elections: You can’t beat someone with no one. And — perhaps more importantly — it’s about the math. Republicans are up first with elections in both chambers starting Tuesday morning. THE HITCHHIKER’S GUIDE TO WHAT HAPPENS NEXT ON CAPITOL HILL For Minority Leader, House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., is running against Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio. Current House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., is not seeking to stay in leadership once his party isn't in charge anymore. If Democrats have 260 seats, Republicans would have 175. All incoming House Republicans (including nonvoting delegates from U.S. territories) are allowed to vote in conference. The selection of minority leader does NOT go before the entire House like speaker. So, the winning candidate only needs a simple majority. That would be 88. The same for the race between House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., and Rep. August Pfluger, R-Texas, for Minority Whip. Senate Republican leader John Thune, R-S.D., is running to keep his leadership position for the party in the new Congress. Meanwhile, Democrats will begin elections for their House leader on Wednesday, when Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., is expected to secure that nomination. No internal Democrat Senate leadership election date has been set. There are some progressives and Democratic Socialists of America-affiliated Democrats who will be House members next year who want someone other than Minority Leader Jeffries keep his position. Who do they want instead? Well, no one has said. Again, you can’t beat someone with no one. And frankly, it’s hard to believe that Democrats would not elect the first Black speaker of the House. But drill down on the math. For the sake of argument, let’s say Democrats have 260 House seats in the new Congress. First, Democrats must tap a nominee for speaker in their caucus. That needs a simple majority. So surely Jeffries will score at least 131 votes in a private ballot for speaker. The speaker of the House is the Constitutional officer for the legislative branch of government – much like the President is for the executive branch and the Chief Justice of the United States for the judicial branch. Thus, the ENTIRE House votes for speaker when it convenes the new Congress at noon on January 3. There are 435 members. If all members cast ballots, Jeffries simply needs 218. Jeffries could lose 40 votes or so and still prevail. So that is not going to happen. He might not even lose more than a couple votes, frankly. The Senate Democratic Caucus and Republican Conference work much the same way as the House. A simple majority wins for majority leader in the Democratic Caucus and minority leader in the Republican Conference. However, the selection of Senate majority leader is not a vote which plays out on the floor. The concept of "Senate Majority Leader" has only been around since the early 20th century and is not mentioned in the Constitution. Remember what we said about the House Speaker being the head of this branch of government. It would be hard to envision a scenario where Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., would not become Majority Leader after Democrats flipped the Senate in a beatdown. First, who else is running? Well, Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, is very popular among Senate Democrats. But he’s running for Majority Whip to succeed retiring Senate Minority Whip Dick Durbin, D-Ill. One could see Democrats defaulting to Schatz if something happens with Schumer. Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., said he wants to look at his options and endorsed Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., for majority leader. But Van Hollen isn’t running. Sen.-elect Annie Andrews, D-S.C., told colleague Bret Baier she wants a "generational change" in leadership. Sen.-elect Troy Jackson, D-Maine, and Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton, D-Kan., both said they would oppose Schumer. But again, you can’t beat someone with no one. REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: HOW MIDTERMS MAY CHANGE THE HOUSE IMPEACHMENT EQUATION FOR HEGSETH Here’s the math: Let’s say Democrats do win Mississippi and Alaska, giving them 56 senators who caucus with the Democrats. All Schumer needs is 29 Democrats to support him in caucus, and he’s the next majority leader. There has not been as much rumbling about the future of Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D. Heretofore, President Trump has not called for new leadership in the Senate. But a group of Senate Republicans are calling on a delay in leadership elections slated for Tuesday. Senate Republicans would choose Thune or anyone else on a secret ballot in the Senate GOP Conference. A simple majority would win. If Republicans are down to 44 seats, the winner would just need 23 votes. So for the next couple of weeks, there’s a lot of counting. Counting about votes for impeachment. Counting in leadership elections. And next year, counting votes as Democrats try to enact their agenda. Democrats will say voters are counting on them. And Republicans, well, they may be counting the days. Everything in the new Congress will come down to the math. And there's the issue of impeaching Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth. But forget about Democrats pushing the move next year. Try Republicans — THIS year. Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., is reintroducing articles of impeachment for Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth this week. The chances are increasingly high that the House could in fact impeach Hegseth. Why? Massie tried to impeach Hegseth before the midterms. But the House adjourned a day early in September. That nixed Massie’s effort. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) condemned the effort by the Kentucky Republican. But Johnson insisted that he didn’t send members home early because of fear that the House had the votes to impeach Hegseth. Massie attempted to execute a parliamentary move which would compel the House to consider the impeachment articles right away. But they expired once the House went out of session. But Massie will resuscitate them. GOP LAWMAKER SAYS MORE QUALIFIED OFFICIALS SHOULD LEAD PENTAGON, QUESTIONS HEGSETH'S 'MORAL COMPASS Massie authored a total of eight articles of impeachment, ranging from the "kidnapping" of Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro to how the Pentagon is running the war in Iran. It’s possible the House could move to table the articles, or send them to committee, euthanizing the effort. But a growing number of House Republicans are grumbling about Hegseth. Any effort to dismiss the articles in the House might not work. It’s about the math. All Democrats are likely to vote to impeach Hegseth. Some Republicans are exasperated by Hegseth and have said privately they’d like to impeach. There are even more Republicans trying to build distance between themselves and President Trump after the midterms. That’s augmented by the fact that Republicans believe the war in Iran cost them control of Congress. Thus, even more Republicans may be willing to impeach. Finally, the GOP may have attendance problems. Republican members who lost – or were shocked that they lost – might not show up. In other words, there may be more Democrats in the House than Republicans. And don’t forget that some Republicans are now looking for a scapegoat after the election. A simple majority is necessary to impeach. If adopted, the House would send the articles of impeachment to the Senate. Under Senate rules of impeachment, the Senate must at least receive and consider the articles. But it could move quickly to dismiss. That’s what happened when the Senate considered articles of impeachment for former Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas a few years ago. The bona fide "trial" part of the process never happened where the Senate heard arguments, listened to witnesses and took evidence. It takes a simple majority to dismiss such articles. Believe it or not, this could happen under a Republican-controlled Senate. But how might outgoing Sens. John Cornyn, R-Texas, Thom Tillis, R-N.C., and Bill Cassidy, R-La., vote? That’s to say nothing of Sens. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, John Curtis, R-Alaska, Todd Young, R-Ind., and others. It takes a two-thirds vote to convict and remove in a Senate impeachment trial. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In addition, unlike legislation, articles of impeachment carry over into the new Congress. Would a new Democratically-controlled Senate want to get bogged down in an impeachment trial from the start? Especially when new Democrats want to vote on affordability and healthcare? Or, would a Democratic Senate embrace the idea of a full-blown impeachment trial for Hegseth – especially since the execution of the war in Iran seems to be one of the main reasons for this week’s electoral shellacking? Some of this hinges on who both parties in each body select as their leaders.

articles.title: Trump defends Pentagon chief as Massie targets him: 'Hegseth should be praised, not impeached'
articles.summary: President Donald Trump is defending War Secretary Pete Hegseth as GOP Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky targets the Pentagon chief for impeachment.
articles.body: President Donald Trump is defending War Secretary Pete Hegseth as outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., targets the Pentagon chief for impeachment. The president issued a Truth Social post on Monday slamming the congressman as "a total loser" while asserting that the war secretary "should be praised, not impeached." "Defeated Republican Congressman Thomas Massie, a total loser, is trying to Impeach perhaps the most popular and successful military official in the Country, Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth," Trump declared Monday on Truth Social. HEGSETH IMPEACHMENT VOTE LOOMS AS HOUSE REPUBLICANS PRIVATELY WARN IT COULD PASS "With recruitment at an ALL-TIME HIGH, from an all-time low under Sleepy Joe Biden, and TWO VICTORIES, Venezuela and Iran, Pete Hegseth should be praised, not Impeached. Congress, stand up for Pete!!!" he added. Massie did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's comment request on Tuesday. Hegseth shared a screenshot of the president's post and thanked him. REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: HOW MIDTERMS MAY CHANGE THE HOUSE IMPEACHMENT EQUATION FOR HEGSETH "Thank you Mr. President. Like you, we will never back down," Hegseth wrote. Massie, who has served in the House of Representatives since late 2012, lost the GOP primary earlier this year in Kentucky's 4th Congressional District to Trump-backed challenger Ed Gallrein, a former Navy SEAL who went on to win the seat during the general election. "My effort to impeach Secretary Hegseth is a much gentler version of what's coming when the Democrats assume control of the House and Senate next year," Massie said, according to a press release. "They will hold hearings and trials. President Trump should replace Secretary Hegseth now while he can still get a replacement confirmed in the Senate." articles.title: Thomas Massie introduces articles of impeachment against Pete Hegseth as GOP criticism over the Iran war mounts after midterm rout
articles.summary: President Trump has praised his defense secretary since the election, but Republicans who blame the war for their losses are calling for him to go.
articles.body:
Rep. Thomas Massie, a Republican from Kentucky, reintroduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday, alleging that the embattled Pentagon chief had committed "high crimes and misdemeanors" and abused the power of his office by violating the War Powers Resolution, conducting military operations without congressional authorization and ordering unlawful military actions in several countries.

The expected impeachment filing came as Congress returned to Washington, D.C. , to begin a lame-duck session following the historic rout that the GOP suffered in last week's midterm elections .

Hegseth is facing intense political backlash over the United States' costly and unpopular war with Iran, which some top Republicans — including Trump — blame in part for the drubbing that cost them control of Congress.

Hegseth said on Monday that he's "not worried about" the impeachment efforts. The defense secretary said he would address the topic at a press conference on Tuesday morning. It would be Hegseth's first news conference from the Pentagon in six months.

"Despite the absence of a declaration of war, specific statutory authorization, or a national emergency created by an attack upon the United States," Massie said in a speech on the House floor, "Secretary Hegseth knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders to initiate war against a foreign nation."

Massie said Hegseth "has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law."

His actions thus "warrant impeachment and trial, removal from office and disqualification to hold and enjoy any office of honor, trust or profit under the United States," the Kentucky Republican said.

President Trump has pledged to support Hegseth while he faces impeachment.

In a Truth Social post Monday night, Trump defended Hegseth as "the most popular and successful military official" in the country, adding, "Pete Hegseth should be praised, not Impeached. Congress, stand up for Pete!!!"

Earlier, Trump told CNN at a White House press conference he would "stand by him," saying that he believes Massie "has a lot of hatred in his heart."

Massie — who in May lost his bid for reelection to Ed Gallrein, a Trump-backed challenger, in the GOP primary — first introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth in September. But House Speaker Mike Johnson later canceled the final scheduled voting day before the midterm recess, delaying a vote.

It's unclear whether an impeachment effort will succeed in the House, which is still under Republican control, but Massie told ABC News that he's "confident there will be enough GOP defectors for it to pass." To do so, the resolution requires a simple majority, meaning that just three Republicans would need to vote with all Democrats to prevail. A vote could come as soon as this week.

Trump has repeatedly insisted that he is not considering replacing his Pentagon chief, at least not yet.

"No, I think he's doing a very good job," Trump told reporters last week.

The president also said he was unaware of a report that Hegseth has been quietly angling to fill the U.S. Senate seat that will be vacated by Tennessee GOP Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who was elected as the state's next governor.

"I think he's doing a very good job, and I actually think he'd be very popular if he did that. But I haven't heard that at all," Trump said when asked if he would want the defense secretary to fill Blackburn's seat.

CBS News , however, reported last week that Trump "has been asking advisers" whether he should stay or go.

Hegseth, a former Fox News host who has served as defense secretary since January 2025, has been Trump's most visible cheerleader for the Iran war, which the U.S. and Israel initiated in February and which has led to surging oil prices.

He has also been among the advisers urging Trump to restart the war. He and Adm. Brad Cooper, the head of U.S. Central Command, have supported a return to major combat operations against Iran during recent briefings on military options, the Wall Street Journal reported on Nov. 6, while Vice President JD Vance and special envoy Steve Witkoff have pushed for diplomacy to end the conflict.

Trump acknowledged on Nov. 4 that the Iran war had partly contributed to the midterm election rout that handed Democrats control of Congress. Vance was unequivocal.

"The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone," Vance wrote in a lengthy post on X . "The reason we lost is the war."

The vice president did not call out Hegseth by name. But other Republicans did.

Sen. Thom Tillis, a Republican from North Carolina, told CBS News that Hegseth faces "a reckoning."

"He is one of the reasons why we don't have the funding or guarantee for defense that we need," Tillis said on election night. "I think after the election, we need to determine whether or not he's the best person to bring those needs to Congress."

Tillis, who voted to confirm Hegseth last year, recently called on Trump to fire him.

"I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country," Tillis wrote in a scathing assessment of Hegseth on X in September. "He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and well-being of our fighting force. I urge the President to find a new leader at the Pentagon who will retain and empower our military talent rather than diminish it."

Rep. James Comer of Kentucky, the Republican chairman of the House Oversight Committee, said on Nov. 6 that "there's a lot of questions about Hegseth."

"We have no idea what the strategy is moving forward in Iran," Comer told NewsNation . "No one's happy about Iran."

When Democrats take control of both the House and Senate next year, they will have the ability to call for hearings and launch investigations into virtually any aspect of the Trump administration — and Hegseth's handling of the military is high on their list.

"In the majority, one of the first things we're gonna do is run Pete Hegseth out of town," Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the minority leader who is poised to become House speaker in January, said at a rally last month .

Hegseth, for his part, has remained defiant.

In a 5-and-a-half-minute video posted to X on Nov. 5, Hegseth defended the Iran war, touted changes he's implemented as Pentagon chief ("We ended the weird and the woke") and praised Trump's leadership while dismissing Massie's impeachment pursuit.

"A disgruntled, defeated congressman along with all his Democrat allies has dropped sham impeachment articles against yours truly," Hegseth said. "It didn't work with President Trump and it won't work with me."
