articles.title: Kushner enters Ukraine peace talks as Trump eyes securing safeguards against another Russian invasion
articles.summary: Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff push a NATO-like security guarantee for Ukraine as first trilateral Abu Dhabi talks tackle territory disputes.
articles.body: Russia and Ukraine will finally return to the negotiating table Tuesday for their first trilateral peace talks with the U.S. in nine months. Ahead of the talks, officials said both Moscow and Kyiv have shown "a little bit of flexibility privately" on territorial disputes that have long stood in the way of reaching an agreement. U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff will sit down with Ukrainian intelligence chief Rustem Umerov and Putin aide and veteran negotiator Vladimir Medinsky in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday. The Trump administration has asked Russia to accept an "Article Four and an Article Five-like security guarantee" for Ukraine that would be "effectively very similar to NATO," a U.S. official said Monday on a background call previewing the negotiations. President Donald Trump has not yet decided what security guarantee the U.S. itself would provide, the official said, describing an American guarantee as a "really, really big deal" that would ultimately have to be worked out between Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. RUSSIA'S NEIGHBOR REVEALS PERSONAL APPEALS TO TRUMP AS US WEIGHS NATO TROOP PULLBACK IN EUROPE A lot has happened on the geopolitical stage since the latest trilateral talks happened in Geneva, Switzerland, in February. The first being the inception of a new conflict between the U.S. and Iran — and the second being the 2026 midterm elections, which saw a sweeping rebuke of Republicans with a blue wave taking the country by storm. The latest round of talks will also mark the beginning of structured negotiations over territory. Russia continues publicly to demand all of Donetsk, while Ukraine has pushed for freezing the conflict along the current line of contact. But behind closed doors, "both sides have shown a little bit of flexibility privately," the official said. UKRAINE'S ZELENSKYY OPEN TO FREEZING FRONT LINES IN CEASEFIRE WITH RUSSIA Trump also suggested in a "60 Minutes" interview that aired Sunday that Ukraine’s borders could ultimately change under a peace agreement, saying the country could emerge from the war with "a little bit different shape." U.S. negotiators do not expect to resolve the territorial dispute in Abu Dhabi. Instead, officials say the goal is to clarify where each side stands, identify the remaining gaps and begin exploring potential compromises that can ultimately be taken back to Russian President Vladimir Putin and Zelenskyy. The administration increasingly views the territorial question and postwar security arrangements as inseparable. Officials believe neither Russia nor Ukraine will make the concessions needed to settle the territorial dispute until each understands what the security landscape will look like after the fighting stops. INSIDE MELANIA TRUMP'S SECRET DIPLOMATIC ROLE IN THE RUSSIA-UKRAINE CEASEFIRE DEAL Before sitting down with Russia and Ukraine, U.S. negotiators will meet with national security officials from Germany, France, the United Kingdom and Italy, along with NATO, the European Union and Ukraine, to discuss security guarantees and a broader postwar security architecture. Washington then hopes to persuade Russia to join a broader multilateral negotiating process involving European governments. "We need Europe at the table," a U.S. official said, arguing that direct negotiations between Russia and European countries will ultimately be necessary for a durable settlement. Among the ideas under consideration is reviving the NATO-Russia Council, which the administration wants to make a more robust forum for communication, de-escalation and resolving future disputes. Officials are also exploring crisis communications, greater military transparency and reciprocal measures intended to reduce the risk of another conflict. The administration's goal in Abu Dhabi is not a final agreement. Officials instead hope the talks can establish a framework for more frequent negotiations and eventually move the process from a U.S.-Russia-Ukraine format to broader multilateral talks involving Europe. The administration also sees sanctions as potential leverage in enforcing an eventual agreement. A U.S. official suggested sanctions on Russia could potentially be eased over time while retaining the ability to "spring back in place" if Moscow violates a peace deal. Witkoff and Kushner, the son-in-law of the president, are also considering returning to meet Putin and Zelenskyy soon, depending on the outcome of the Abu Dhabi talks. "This is the first time I feel like we see real desire on the Russian side to finish," the official said. But officials acknowledged the negotiations remain highly uncertain, with deep distrust between Moscow and Kyiv and major decisions on territory and security still unresolved. The immediate test in Abu Dhabi will be whether the private flexibility U.S. negotiators say they are seeing can translate into something concrete once Russia and Ukraine are back in the same room. But the Abu Dhabi talks could also set the stage for higher-level diplomacy. U.S. officials said Witkoff and Kushner are considering returning to meet Putin and Zelenskyy soon, depending on the outcome of the two-day negotiations. Trump is also preparing to travel to China for the APEC summit next week, where he said Sunday he expects to meet Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Discussions about a potential three-way meeting are underway, though no summit has been finalized. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

articles.title: Thousands of voters in Mississippi Senate race are trying to make their ballots count after state’s voter roll changes
articles.summary: In a Senate race that is still too close to call, Mississippi state election officials are facing intense scrutiny over their methods for maintaining voter r...
articles.body:
Andrew Couch had voted at the same polling location in the last two elections. But when he arrived at his polling place on Election Day, he was told he was registered in a different county that he hadn't lived in for six years.

"I couldn't believe that," Couch told CNN. "That was such an old address. I've lived at so many other addresses since then."

He filled out a provisional ballot that night and, in the days since, has taken steps to try to fix the issue and understand what went wrong. But on Monday, he was told his vote will not count.

"I'm very upset," Couch said. "I've been participating in his process for many years as an adult. I've been teaching my kids to participate as well. So, if people lose faith in the process that we're going through, I think it's going to hurt voter turnout in general in the future."

In a Senate race that is still too close to call, Mississippi state election officials are facing intense scrutiny over their methods for maintaining voter rolls after thousands of voters like Couch cast provisional ballots because they were not included in precinct poll books or did not have appropriate photo identification.

Whether those ballots are ultimately counted could determine the outcome of a contest where Democrat Scott Colom is narrowly leading Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith . But the fight over provisional ballots – known as affidavit ballots in Mississippi – is indicative of how Republicans at the federal and state level have zeroed in on voter rolls, in some cases disqualifying voters with scant notice.

Election officials in Mississippi made waves last year when they began using commercially available credit data to identify voters who may have moved as part of voter list maintenance.

Critics of the use of the credit data, which they argue may not be reliable in a state where many residents don't have bank accounts, say they believe it contributed to a surge in voters deemed inactive and then excluded from poll books. Those voters then were required to vote via provisional ballots if they showed up on Election Day.

Tuesday is the deadline for voters who cast provisional ballots because they did not have proper identification to provide the needed documentation to election officials. In interviews with CNN, several county election officials said that voter ID issues accounted for a relatively small share of provisional ballots they issued.

County election officials have until Friday to vet and count all provisional ballots and certify their county-level results. The state certification deadline is December 3.

It's not clear how many Mississippians have voted via provisional ballot. Both camps in the Senate race have said thousands of voters were affected, either because their names were missing in poll books or they lacked adequate identification.

Mississippi's Secretary of State Michael Watson, a Republican, said in a statement to CNN that state officials have "implemented every available resource to ensure our elections are secure, and to ensure we do not have dead people, illegal aliens with fake addresses, or nonresidents voting in our elections."

He said the affidavit ballot process "is a safety net for errors election commissioners make during voter roll maintenance."

"It may take voters a little longer for final results to come in, but more accurate voter lists will speed up the process and decrease opportunities for voter fraud in Mississippi. And in the end, accuracy and integrity will be maintained," he added.

As of Monday evening, Watson said 15,547 affidavit ballots had been processed with roughly 76% of them accepted. Another 2,578 absentee ballots were still outstanding.

Voting rights advocates accused Mississippi of disenfranchising legitimate voters.

"Once you have done the act of registering to vote, which is your constitutional right, then there shouldn't be a purging at any occurrence, you shouldn't be rendered inactive," Mississippi State Director for the Southern Poverty Law Center Waikinya Clanton said. "Voting is about choice and it's about responsibility and so people can choose to engage in a process or not."

The Hinds County Courthouse in Jackson was buzzing with voters all day Monday demanding answers about their ballot. In interviews with CNN this week, several Mississippi voters who were ensnared by the process said they have had to scramble to confirm their votes would count.

TaChana Hurst, a Colom supporter who lives in Hinds County, told CNN she voted the last seven years without issues. But this year, after not being allowed to cast an absentee ballot, she arrived at her polling place only to be told she had to report to a different precinct. After hours of going back and forth between two precincts, she was told to fill out an affidavit ballot that was accepted a few days later.

"I'm just glad that I refused to give up because I could have just left when they couldn't find me in the system, but that wouldn't be exercising my right to vote," she recalled. "I've never had this experience before."

The Mississippi Poor People's Campaign, a grassroots organization, has been coordinating rides to help voters check on their ballots.

In the car on the way to the Hinds County Courthouse on Monday, Rebecca Cavett was clutching her driver's license, as she waited to find out if her ballot was going to be accepted. She wasn't sure if she was given an affidavit or absentee ballot initially, Cavett said, speaking to how chaotic and confusing she found the experience. She found out Monday that she had voted via an absentee ballot but says she was told she needed to provide more identification in person.

She lost her daughter to gun violence and her brother died of prostate cancer after facing mounting medical bills, Cavett said, so she was going to fight for her vote to count for Colom. Cavett's ballot was accepted, but she is worried about others who might give up given how complicated the process has become.

"It's causing voter fatigue. You get discouraged a little bit, but I know that my vote is my voice. So, it's been a whole obstacle course, but it's worth it. It's worth it, and your vote does count," Cavett told CNN.

The secretary of state worked with Experian

Watson, the Mississippi secretary of state, announced last year that the state had reached a deal with the credit reporting agency Experian to provide data as an additional tool to help identify voters who may have moved.

The decision raised concern among some political observers.

Marvin King, who teaches political science and African American Studies at the University of Mississippi, questioned the accuracy of the data, given that more than 9% of the state's residents do not use a bank and are outside the credit system.

Mississippi Today reported that the state's voter maintenance activities had left more than 230,000 voters statewide – or about 1 in 9 – in inactive status ahead of Election Day.

In a statement, an Experian official said the company has not "provided services" to Mississippi since early 2025.

"The solution provided at that time consisted of supplemental address information and was not designed or intended to validate voter records," it added.

The inactive voters have not been removed from the rolls. But Michael Morse, an expert on election administration at the University of Pennsylvania's law school, said the decision to exclude them from poll books that local officials use at each precinct sets Mississippi apart from other jurisdictions.

Many states allow inactive voters who show up at the correct precinct on Election Day to cast a regular ballot rather than vote provisionally, he said. In addition, he noted that federal law allows even voters deemed inactive to remain eligible to vote at their address of registration for two federal general elections.

"Mississippi short-circuits the process by hastily excluding you from the poll book," Morse said.

This story has been updated with additional information.

CNN's Tierney Sneed contributed to this report.

articles.title: Russia? Iran? Who is behind this rash of bomb threats in Europe?
articles.summary: Whether the West is facing Russian hybrid warfare, Iranian terrorism, or both, its collective response has been wholly inadequate.
articles.body:
Last Tuesday , Europe began suffering a wave of bomb threats against commercial passenger airlines, causing delays, confusion and disruption across the continent. This continued on Thursday and Friday . The bomb threats targeted over fifty separate flights, to or from Spain, Italy, Poland, Finland, the United Kingdom and several other countries.

No explosives were found. All passengers, crew and aircraft remained unharmed. Nonetheless, the Europe-wide turmoil was considerable, as were the attendant costs and delays incurred to ensure safety.

Hardest to calculate is the psychological impact of uncertainty and the possible loss of confidence in air transportation or travel generally. Airline hijackings, bombings like Pan Am 103 in 1988 — not to mention 9/11, may have seemed distant memories — but memories quickly revived by last week’s events.

European and national authorities are conducting extensive investigations. On Friday, Ireland faced several bomb threats to media outlets, including its state radio and television broadcaster, RTE. No real bombs were found, but the Irish government nonetheless said publicly that “it seems likely that this is a coordinated campaign of disruption.” Since Ireland is the current president of the European Council, it is the locus for considerable high-level EU activity at the moment.

These provocations are serious. So far, there is no publicly available evidence for which state or terrorist actor was responsible, or for what the objective was. But Russia comes immediately to mind as a potential perpetrator.

Since the Kremlin’s 2014 and 2022 invasions of Ukraine, nearby countries such as Poland, Romania and the Baltics have been subjected to continuing harassment through airplane, missile and drone overflights, not to mention cyberattacks. Moscow has repeatedly denied all such allegations, instead attributing at least some of the overflights and hacks to Ukraine.

In August, explosives-laden drones attacked planes at the Leipzig, Germany commercial airport (also used by NATO for certain purposes). Berlin blamed Moscow, and closed Russia’s consulate in Bonn in response. Russia argued that Germany had invented the incident. Moscow has also repeatedly denied involvement in a series of hacks across Europe in recent weeks against the cold-food supply-chain, sabotaging facilities and ruining considerable quantities of frozen or thawing food.

Another potential perpetrator is Iran — perhaps acting on its own, perhaps coordinating with Russia. Iran has threatened retaliation well outside the Gulf region if the U.S. and Israel resume significant strikes against it. Tehran’s terrorist reach in Europe and America is already well known, and its joint interests with Moscow are a strong incentive to work together. On Monday, France blamed Iran for the attacks on the cold-storage chain.

Whether the West is facing Russian hybrid warfare, Iranian terrorism, or both, its collective response has been wholly inadequate.

First, the bomb threats and other disruptions are being conducted in the seam between NATO’s alliance defense responsibilities and law-enforcement authorities which Europeans still largely retain in national hands. The European Union’s murky authorities only further confuse the picture.

Second, the Trump administration’s focus on U.S. elections has until recently distracted it from foreign matters. This significant and growing pattern of threats, hacks and disruptions is too extensive to ignore or brush aside any longer, even if it only represents probing or testing by Russia .

Unfortunately, there is an even graver problem. In his unending quest for a Nobel Peace Prize, Trump continues pursuing a Russia-Ukraine peace deal. During the 2024 campaign, he said he could solve the war in 24 hours, even before he took office. Always selling, Trump said last week , “It’s going to involve more than Ukraine, and I could even say it might involve all of Europe. It’s going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone’s going to be thrilled.” Details on this thrilling development remain scarce and closely held.

The idea that broad changes to European security arrangements are possible amid ongoing — indeed, accelerating — hybrid warfare by Russia against the West is dubious at best. Instead, today’s threats highlight the fallacy underlying Trump’s entire negotiating approach, whether in Ukraine, Gaza or Iran. It centers on investment opportunities that will supposedly arise once peace is achieved, but without troubling unnecessarily with the messy of problem of how to achieve that peace.

Combatants in every known conflict doubtless hope for massive aid and investment after hostilities end, to rebuild their respective economies. That incentive is universal. The hard point, though, is that until the underlying issues giving rise to the conflict in the first place are resolved, there aren’t going to be any investment deals.

Trump and his negotiators disdain the idea of learning more about the conflicts and the interests at stake — independence and freedom for Ukraine, peace and security for Israel, ending the Iranian terrorist and nuclear threats — because they view this as a form of getting “bogged down.” Good luck with that approach.

Airplane or media bombing threats, food-chain hacks and the like may seem mundane. But if the West fails to deal seriously with the here and now, the consequences will be grave. The U.S. National Security Council and NATO should be addressing these issues urgently, not considering oil deals with Russia.

John Bolton was national security adviser to President Trump from 2018 to 2019 and U.S. ambassador to the United Nations from 2005 to 2006. He held senior State Department posts at times between 1981 and 2005.

articles.title: 4 storylines to watch as Congress dives into lame-duck session
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Congress faces lame-duck test ▪ Nvidia stock slips after probe news ▪ Mississippi Senate race meets deadlines ▪ Russell Brand sentenced to 10.5 years Lawmakers returned to Washington this week with a laundry list of legislative items to push through and a myriad battles brewing. As the lame-duck session gets underway,…
articles.body:
▪ Mississippi Senate race meets deadlines

Lawmakers returned to Washington this week with a laundry list of legislative items to push through and a myriad battles brewing.

As the lame-duck session gets underway, here are some notable storylines to watch.

Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) filed articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth yesterday, which could potentially force a vote on the Pentagon chief’s fate as soon as this week.

The articles accuse Hegseth of “high crimes and misdemeanors” related to the Iran war and to the deaths of hundreds of civilians in boat strikes in the Caribbean against alleged drug smugglers. Massie first introduced the impeachment articles in September, but Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) adjourned before a vote could come to the floor.

Hegseth will hold a press conference about the effort today at 8 a.m. EST. It will be his first press conference in more than six months.

The impeachment push is gaining steam on Capitol Hill, where even some House Republicans are weighing whether to support the resolution after Democrats triumphed in the midterms last week, with exit polling showing the Iran war was a major factor.

Even if Massie has the votes in the House, GOP leaders may look for a way to avoid a trial in the Senate during this Congress.

Some Senate Republicans are urging their conference to delay the party’s leadership elections, which are scheduled for today.

Sen. Dave McCormick (R-Pa.), a moderate from a key battleground state, joined his conservative GOP colleagues in calling on Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) not to rush into leadership elections without first reflecting on “what went wrong” in the midterms, “how we fix it, what we stand for, and how our agenda must focus on the concerns of the American people.”

The Hill’s Alexander Bolton reports for The Hill Insider that Senate Budget Committee Chair Ron Johnson (R-Wis.) and other conservatives want to delay the leadership elections to extract more leverage over the GOP lame-duck agenda.

They say that could put them in a better position to push through a reconciliation package and potentially cancel the Thanksgiving recess if necessary.

The Senate voted yesterday to advance a major bipartisan bill that aims to speed up the construction of energy and other infrastructure projects.

Supporters of the legislation see the lame-duck session as the best shot to pass permitting reform, since they do not expect the next Democratic-led Congress to be able to reach a deal with the Trump administration.

Some Democrats, including House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), have expressed concerns about the bill’s impact on environmental and tribal laws, which could prove to be an obstacle to getting the package through both chambers.

President Trump also tossed an apparent curveball into the process on Monday, saying he opposed a provision of the bill incentivizing wind turbine buildout. Senate passage is not guaranteed, but the 73-25 vote on Monday makes it likely.

House Republicans are also gearing up to elect a new leadership team today that will have to navigate the conference’s transition to the minority party, as some GOP members say the election losses last week require a shake-up at the top of leadership.

Sudiksha Kochi has a look for The Hill Insider at how the contests for the some of the top spots are shaping up, with House Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) challenging House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) for minority leader.

Republican Study Committee Chair August Pfluger (Texas) has announced a challenge against House GOP Whip Tom Emmer (Minn.), while Republican Reps. Greg Steube (Fla.) and Erin Houchin (Ind.) are challenging current GOP Conference Chair Lisa McClain (Mich.) for her post.

But there has similarly been a push to delay the leadership election on the House side. House Ways and Means Committee Chair Jason Smith (R-Mo.) said it’s too soon to make a decision today about the direction of the party, arguing leadership elections should be delayed “until we decide how to hold each other accountable and what our path forward should be.”

Speaker Johnson has not endorsed either candidate to replace him, and Trump has said he plans to stay out of the leadership elections.

▪ The Hill : James Talarico , John Cornyn meet in Washington.

▪ The Hill : Hegseth orders major revamp of military education.

The Supreme Court allowed border barrier construction to continue in and around Big Bend National Park in Texas, in a significant win for the Trump administration. The high court halted a lower court decision to pause the construction as the underlying case played out.

Three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States opened Tuesday in the United Arab Emirates. Trump’s son-in-law and global envoy, Jared Kushner, expressed optimism about potential progress, though expectations for a breakthrough remain low.

Trump downplayed the possibility of renewed military action against Iran but said the U.S. would maintain its wartime posture in the Middle East to protect Arab and Gulf allies. The president’s comments followed a meeting with Iran’s primary interlocutor, Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang listens as President Donald Trump speaks during an event at the U.S. Institute of Peace, Oct. 8, 2026, in Washington. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson, Associated Press)

TOOK A TUMBLE: Nvidia shares slipped 5 percent after the opening bell yesterday following news that the chipmaker opened an investigation into reports that its CEO, Jensen Huang , was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.”

Huang acknowledged on Sunday that he had been intimate with a business executive who U.S. intelligence says was spying for China, according to The New York Times. The Chinse foreign ministry denied the allegations as a smear campaign.

Nvidia’s board said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised,” but said its “inquiry will examine all available information.”

Nvidia is central to the artificial intelligence race, and its chips power many of the data centers and computing systems that train AI models. A spokesperson for the company said Huang will continue to lead the company during the investigation, and Huang said he supports the review and will cooperate fully with it.

Trump defended Huang in brief remarks Sunday evening, telling reporters, “I haven’t heard he’s done anything wrong,” and that “I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what’s going on.”

The president added that he would “certainly” take Huang on his upcoming trip to China.

▪ The Hill : Who is Jensen Huang, CEO facing probe over affair with alleged spy.

▪ The Hill : Top Dem demands probe into Huang’s affair.

DEADLINE DAY : Mississippi’s too-close-to-call Senate race between GOP incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democrat Scott Colom will come into greater focus today.

Today is the deadline for counting provisional ballots — or “affidavit ballots,” as they’re called in Mississippi — which voters can request when their identities cannot be verified at the polls. Before provisional ballots can be counted in Mississippi, they must be processed and verified. Today is also the deadline to receive absentee ballots by mail that are postmarked by Election Day.

The results must be certified by all 82 counties by Friday, at which point a lawsuit can be filed, since there is no automatic vote recount in close races or path to challenge the results in the state.

Colom leads Hyde-Smith by roughly 2,700 votes, according to Decision Desk HQ’s (DDHQ) tally. Alaska’s Senate race is also too close to call, with roughly 70 percent of the vote in and Democrat Mary Peltola leading Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan by 637 votes in the latest DDHQ tally.

▪ The Hill : Colom calls out election raters for writing off his Senate campaign.

▪ The Hill : Sullivan campaign files motion over rejected absentee ballot lawsuit.

FOURTH DOWN: The Department of Justice lost its fourth top official in the week since the midterm elections, with Assistant Attorney General for the Civil Division Brett Shumate resigning yesterday, The Hill’s Rebecca Beitsch reports .

The Civil Division handles a wide range of cases and has seen departures soar under the Trump administration amid an uptick in caseloads.

Harmeet Dhillon , who led the Civil Rights Division, was the first to depart after the election. U.S. Attorney Jason Reding Quiñones , whose South Florida district oversaw the sweeping probe of the investigations into Trump, and John Eisenberg , assistant attorney general for the National Security Division, both resigned Friday.

▪ The Hill : Sonia Sotomayor hopes SCOTUS overturns presidential immunity decision.

The president holds executive time, a photo opportunity and policy meetings.

Florida Democratic Party Chair Nikki Fried is interviewed by a reporter before President Joe Biden’s appearance during a reproductive freedom campaign event at Hillsborough Community College, April 23, 2024, in Tampa, Fla. (Phelan M. Ebenhack, Associated Press file)

BATTLEGROUND AGAIN? As Democrats swept last week’s elections, including in several GOP strongholds, Florida remained something of an outlier, electing Republicans to the governor’s mansion and Senate.

But Florida Democratic Party chair Nikki Fried is pushing back against the narrative that her state’s elections results brought only bad news. Instead, she is taking a victory lap, using the election results to make the case to national Democratic operatives and donors that Democrats are not a lost cause in the state.

In an interview with The Hill’s Amie Parnes , Fried recounts telling Democratic operatives in recent days that “Yes, we could win … Imagine if we put a little more into Florida.”

Democrats may not have won statewide last week, but they did make significant inroads.

Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Fla.) won reelection by nearly 3 percentage points last week — a much narrower margin than when Secretary of State Marco Rubio won his Senate reelection bid by more than 16 points in 2022.

Similarly, Florida Gov.-elect Byron Donalds (R)won his election last week by a little more than 1 point, whereas Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) won by nearly 20 points in 2022.

Fried also noted that Democrats made progress elsewhere in the Sunshine State last week.

Democrats flipped 16 Republican-held state House seats and another in the state Senate, Fried noted. The party also broke the Republican supermajority in the Florida House, and Democratic candidates are on track to hold on to the four congressional seats redistricted to favor the GOP.

Florida Democrats, Fried told Parnes, “created all of this by our sheer grit.”

▪ The Hill : Where all 18 unprojected House races stand.

Comedian and actor Russell Brand is reflected in a car window as he leaves Southwark Crown Court in London, Nov. 2, 2026, where he is charged with counts of rape and sexual assault against six women. (Alberto Pezzali, Associated Press)

BRAND BEHIND BARS: Actor Russell Brand was sentenced to 10 and a half years in prison for raping a woman and sexually assaulting three others at a time when his stardom was on the rise.

Brand maintained his innocence throughout the trial and testified that all his encounters were consensual. He was cleared of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

The prosecutor in the case said Brand “abused the influence and power that came with his fame” and “used it to facilitate access to women without which the offending could not have taken place. It also fed his own view that he could commit such offenses with impunity.”

Brand has become an antiestablishment flag-bearer and a prominent figure in the “Make America Healthy Again” movement. After a jury found Brand guilty last week, former Fox News host Megyn Kelly went live on her YouTube page to express her dismay at the verdict.

“I don’t believe the charge… and I don’t have to believe them just because the jury came through with the opposite conclusion,” Kelly said, adding, “I feel indignant that this obvious conservative stalwart has been targeted.”

Elon Musk similarly weighed in on a post mocking Brand’s conviction of a crime more than a decade after it happened, saying the fact that England does not have a statute of limitations for rape or sexual assault is “a crazy legal standard.”

▪ The Hill : White House staff treated Trump like a ‘baby’: Calley Means .

Protecting America’s digital infrastructure starts with common sense , Rep. Rich McCormick (R-Ga.) writes in The Hill.

Democrats must not cede power via permitting bill that would fast-track data centers , Kenny Bruno writes in The Hill.

The Jimmy Carter Boyhood Farm is seen, Dec. 30, 2024, in Archery, Ga. Former President Jimmy Carter died Sunday at the age of 100. (Mike Stewart, Associated Press)

And finally … Former President Jimmy Carter ’s family farm in Georgia was sold to The Conservation Fund for $8.5 million, with plans to preserve the land and eventually open it up to the public.

“We’re honored to help ensure this land remains [a] healthy habitat for wildlife, and we look forward to the day it is open to everyone who wants to experience it,” said Stacy Funderburke , the organization’s vice president for the central Southeast region.

The nonprofit plans to transfer the property to the Georgia Department of Natural Resources in 2028. The land could open to the public for hunting, fishing and other outdoor activities as early as 2027.

articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth will speak to reporters Tuesday morning as he faces mounting impeachment pressure.

The remarks, marking the first Pentagon press conference in about six months, come a day after Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) on Monday unveiled eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth. Massie has accused the defense chief of violating the Constitution and other laws with U.S. military operations in Iran and elsewhere.

Hegseth dismissed the effort, saying he was “not worried,” while Massie is moving to force a House vote on the measure. President Trump backed his defense secretary during an impromptu briefing Monday, attacking the Kentucky Republican as a “ stone cold loser .” Trump also addressed the conflict with Iran, declaring that the war is “militarily effectively over” and suggesting the U.S. will not resume its bombing campaign unless provoked. The president had earlier met with Qatar’s prime minister.

The House and Senate GOP are set to hold their leadership elections Tuesday, a week after Democrats’ sweeping midterm victories. There are calls in both chambers for a delay.

articles.title: Pedro Sánchez carga contra Abascal por su comentario a Broncano en 'La Revuelta': “Amenazar sonriendo no es hacer humor”
articles.standfirst: El presidente del Gobierno critica la respuesta del líder de Vox al presentador tras la entrevista en TVE
articles.summary: El presidente del Gobierno critica la respuesta del líder de Vox al presentador tras la entrevista en TVE
articles.body: El presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, ha reaccionado al intercambio entre Santiago Abascal y David Broncano al final de la entrevista del líder de Vox en 'La Revuelta'. En un mensaje, Sánchez ha cuestionado el comentario y ha defendido a los profesionales de la comunicación frente a las intimidaciones. “Amenazar sonriendo no es hacer humor, es degradar nuestra democracia”, ha escrito el jefe del Ejecutivo. También ha añadido: “Para esto luchamos: para que España no vuelva a ser un país donde los ultraderechistas amenacen a cómicos y periodistas”. Sánchez ha cerrado su publicación con una llamada a la movilización: “Frente a la involución, movilización” La reacción llega después de que Abascal visitara el programa presentado por Broncano en una entrevista marcada por los reproches y la tensión. El intercambio se produjo durante la despedida, cuando el presentador se dirigió al líder de Vox: “Santiago, no te voy a desear suerte”. Abascal respondió: “Yo a ti sí, porque la vas a necesitar”. Broncano le preguntó a qué se refería. “Es una broma”, contestó el dirigente de Vox, antes de añadir que a veces le salía “un punto de cómico” que, en su opinión, el presentador había perdido durante la entrevista. El cierre de la conversación entre Broncano y Abascal, ha generado reacciones políticas y comentarios en redes sociales. Algunos usuarios han interpretado las palabras de Abascal como una advertencia sobre el futuro profesional de Broncano, mientras que otros las han considerado una respuesta irónica dentro del tono del intercambio.Sánchez ha puesto el foco en el efecto intimidatorio que atribuye a la frase y ha vinculado el episodio con la defensa de la libertad de expresión y el trabajo de periodistas y humoristas. Su mensaje se concentra en las palabras pronunciadas por Abascal durante la despedida.
